clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 58-year-old male admitted to the emergency department with substernal chest pressure radiating to the left jaw for 45 minutes.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Diaphoretic, anxious, pale skin, S4 heart sound auscultated, lungs clear bilaterally.

diagnostic_results.12-lead ECG: ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V4

provider_orders: Prepare for emergent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse prioritize immediately after administering sublingual nitroglycerin to this client?

options.text: Reassess blood pressure and chest pain intensity within 5 minutes
Obtain a repeat 12-lead electrocardiogram in 30 minutes
Administer metoprolol 50 mg orally with a full glass of water
Place the client in a supine position with legs elevated

rationales.summary: Sublingual nitroglycerin acts within 1 to 3 minutes and causes potent vasodilation, requiring blood pressure and symptom reassessment at 5 minutes before considering repeat dosing.
rationales.A: Correct. Nitroglycerin can cause abrupt hypotension; blood pressure and pain score must be checked 5 minutes after each dose.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Waiting 30 minutes delays evaluation of acute hemodynamic response and potential hypotension.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Oral beta-blockers are not given immediately without verifying hemodynamic stability and withholding oral intake prior to emergent PCI.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Supine positioning increases preload and myocardial oxygen demand; semi-Fowler positioning is preferred unless hypotensive.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 72-year-old female with chronic systolic heart failure (LVEF 30%) being discharged home after acute decompensation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Bibasilar lung fields clear, trace ankle edema, alert and oriented.
provider_orders: Discharge home with heart failure self-management teaching

questions.stem: Which statements by the client indicate a correct understanding of heart failure discharge teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: I will weigh myself every morning after urinating and before eating breakfast.
I will call my provider if I gain 3 pounds in 2 days or 5 pounds in a week.
I can use salt substitutes containing potassium chloride freely to flavor my food.
I will take my furosemide in the morning so it does not interrupt my sleep.
I should stop taking carvedilol if I feel mildly tired during the first week.

rationales.summary: Consistent morning weights, early reporting of fluid retention thresholds, and morning loop diuretic timing are essential self-management behaviors in heart failure.
rationales.A: Correct. Weighing at the same time each morning on the same scale after voiding and before eating provides the most accurate fluid balance measurement.
rationales.B: Correct. Weight gain of 2-3 lb in 1-2 days or 5 lb in 1 week indicates early fluid retention requiring medication adjustment.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) retains potassium; potassium-based salt substitutes can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.
rationales.D: Correct. Morning dosing prevents nocturia and sleep disruption.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Beta-blockers like carvedilol should never be stopped abruptly due to rebound tachycardia and ischemia risk.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 66-year-old male on telemetry post-coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) day 2.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Suddenly becomes lightheaded and diaphoretic; palpable radial pulse is weak and rapid.

diagnostic_results.Telemetry: Wide-complex regular tachycardia with a palpable pulse (monomorphic ventricular tachycardia)

questions.stem: Which intervention should the nurse prepare to perform immediately?

options.text: Synchronized cardioversion
Unsynchronized defibrillation
Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push
Carotid sinus massage

rationales.summary: Unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse requires immediate synchronized cardioversion per ACLS guidelines.
rationales.A: Correct. The client has a pulse but demonstrates hemodynamic instability (BP 78/46 mmHg, lightheadedness, diaphoresis), requiring immediate synchronized cardioversion.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Unsynchronized defibrillation is reserved for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation; delivering an unsynchronized shock on a pulse can induce R-on-T ventricular fibrillation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Adenosine is used for stable narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia, not unstable wide-complex ventricular tachycardia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Vagal maneuvers are contraindicated in unstable wide-complex tachycardia and risky in post-CABG patients with potential carotid atherosclerosis.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 69-year-old male with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) of the bilateral lower extremities.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Diminished dorsalis pedis pulses (1+), hair loss on lower legs, thick toenails, pain in calves after walking one block.

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse include when teaching this client how to promote arterial blood flow to the lower extremities?

options.text: Keep the legs in a neutral or slightly dependent position while resting
Elevate the legs on two pillows above heart level whenever seated
Apply a heating pad directly to the feet each evening to warm the skin
Wear knee-high elastic compression stockings throughout the day

rationales.summary: Gravity assists arterial perfusion into distal extremities in PAD, whereas elevation and compression further compromise arterial inflow.
rationales.A: Correct. Neutral or dependent positioning uses gravity to enhance arterial blood flow to ischemic lower extremities.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Elevating legs above heart level reduces arterial perfusion and worsens ischemic rest pain (appropriate for venous insufficiency, not PAD).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Decreased sensory perception increases the risk of severe thermal burns from direct heating pads.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Compression stockings impair already diminished arterial circulation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 52-year-old female receiving a continuous unfractionated heparin infusion for an acute proximal left femoral deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Left calf warm and swollen; no active bleeding noted.

diagnostic_results.Venous Doppler: Occlusive thrombus in left superficial femoral vein

medications: Heparin sodium 25,000 units in 250 mL D5W infusing at 1,300 units/hr

questions.stem: Based on the client's current aPTT result, which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Pause the heparin infusion per protocol and assess for signs of bleeding
Administer protamine sulfate 50 mg IV push immediately
Increase the heparin infusion rate by 200 units/hr
Continue the current infusion rate and recheck aPTT in 24 hours

rationales.summary: An aPTT of 118 seconds exceeds the therapeutic target (60-80 seconds), placing the client at high hemorrhage risk and requiring immediate infusion hold and bleeding assessment.
rationales.A: Correct. Standard heparin protocols require holding the infusion temporarily (typically 30-60 minutes), assessing for occult or overt bleeding, and reducing the infusion rate.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Protamine sulfate is reserved for severe, life-threatening heparin-induced hemorrhage, not an asymptomatic supratherapeutic aPTT.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Increasing the rate would dangerously worsen anticoagulation.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Continuing a supratherapeutic infusion without adjustment risks major hemorrhage.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 49-year-old male admitted to the ICU step-down unit with hypertensive emergency and acute kidney injury.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports throbbing occipital headache and blurred vision; no focal motor deficits.
medications: Nicardipine continuous IV infusion initiated at 5 mg/hr
provider_orders: Titrate nicardipine to reduce MAP by no more than 20-25% in the first hour

questions.stem: Why must the nurse avoid lowering this client's mean arterial pressure (MAP) too rapidly during the first hour of therapy?

options.text: Rapid blood pressure reduction can precipitate cerebral, myocardial, or renal ischemia
Nicardipine causes severe reflex bradycardia and third-degree heart block
Abrupt vasodilation triggers acute hyperkalemia from intracellular shifts
Rapid MAP reduction induces rebound pulmonary hypertension

rationales.summary: Chronic severe hypertension shifts cerebral and renal autoregulation curves upward; abrupt normalization drops perfusion pressure below autoregulatory thresholds.
rationales.A: Correct. Reducing MAP by more than 25% in the first hour compromises cerebral, coronary, and renal autoregulation, risking watershed stroke or acute tubular necrosis.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers like nicardipine typically cause mild reflex tachycardia rather than heart block.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Nicardipine does not cause acute hyperkalemia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Systemic vasodilation does not trigger rebound pulmonary hypertension.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 36-year-old male admitted with fever, night sweats, and a new regurgitant mitral murmur.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Painful erythematous nodules on finger pads (Osler nodes) and splinter hemorrhages under fingernails.

diagnostic_results.Transthoracic Echocardiogram: Mobile vegetation on anterior mitral valve leaflet

medications: Vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours (pending blood cultures)
provider_orders: Obtain 3 sets of blood cultures from separate venipuncture sites before starting IV antibiotics

questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate when implementing the plan of care for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Draw all three sets of blood cultures prior to infusing the first dose of vancomycin.
Monitor the client closely for sudden neurological changes or flank pain.
Educate the client on the need for prophylactic antibiotics prior to invasive dental procedures.
Discontinue IV antibiotic therapy once the client has been afebrile for 48 hours.
Prepare for a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) for long-term outpatient IV therapy.

rationales.summary: Infective endocarditis management centers on pre-antibiotic blood cultures, systemic emboli surveillance, prolonged IV therapy via central access, and future dental prophylaxis.
rationales.A: Correct. Drawing blood cultures before antibiotics prevents false-negative pathogen identification.
rationales.B: Correct. Friable valvular vegetations can embolize to the brain (stroke), kidneys (flank pain/hematuria), or spleen.
rationales.C: Correct. History of infective endocarditis is a high-risk indication for antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Infective endocarditis requires 4 to 6 weeks of continuous IV bactericidal therapy to eradicate organisms embedded in fibrin vegetations.
rationales.E: Correct. Multi-week IV antibiotic courses typically require a PICC line.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 61-year-old female 6 hours post-percutaneous mitral valve repair.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Restless, cool extremities, jugular venous distension to the angle of the jaw, muffled heart sounds.

diagnostic_results.Bedside Ultrasound: Large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse

medications: 0.9% Sodium Chloride IV bolus 500 mL running
provider_orders: STAT cardiology consult for emergent pericardiocentesis

questions.stem: Which classic triad of assessment findings (Beck triad) is demonstrated in this client's presentation?

options.text: Hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds
Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Fever, chest pain relieved by leaning forward, and pericardial friction rub
Widened pulse pressure, bounding pulses, and bibasilar crackles

rationales.summary: Beck triad is the hallmark clinical presentation of acute cardiac tamponade resulting from pericardial fluid compressing the cardiac chambers.
rationales.A: Correct. Hypotension (narrowed pulse pressure), jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds constitute Beck triad.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations describe Cushing triad (increased intracranial pressure).
rationales.C: Incorrect. These findings characterize acute uncomplicated pericarditis.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Widened pulse pressure and bounding pulses are seen in aortic regurgitation or early distributive shock, whereas tamponade causes narrowed pulse pressure.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 74-year-old female with persistent atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc score 4) starting oral anticoagulation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Irregularly irregular apical pulse at 78 bpm, no peripheral edema.

diagnostic_results.ECG: Atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response

questions.stem: Which dietary instruction should the nurse provide to this client regarding warfarin therapy?

options.text: Maintain a consistent daily intake of foods containing vitamin K rather than eliminating them
Strictly avoid all green leafy vegetables, broccoli, and soybeans while taking warfarin
Increase intake of spinach and kale whenever minor gum bleeding occurs
Take warfarin with grapefruit juice each morning to enhance intestinal absorption

rationales.summary: Warfarin antagonizes vitamin K-dependent clotting factors; stable vitamin K intake allows predictable dosing without wide INR fluctuations.
rationales.A: Correct. Consistent intake of vitamin K-rich foods keeps INR stable within the 2.0-3.0 therapeutic range.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Complete elimination deprives the client of nutrients and makes INR overly sensitive to incidental vitamin K exposure.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Self-adjusting vitamin K intake to treat bleeding is unsafe; bleeding requires provider evaluation and INR testing.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP enzymes and interacts with diltiazem, risking hypotension and bradycardia.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 78-year-old male 12 hours after permanent dual-chamber pacemaker insertion via the left subclavian vein.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Dressing over left infraclavicular incision is dry and intact; client reports mild incisional soreness (3/10).

diagnostic_results.Chest X-ray: Atrial and ventricular leads properly positioned; no pneumothorax

medications: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN pain
Cefazolin 1 g IV every 8 hours x 2 doses
provider_orders: Immobilize left shoulder with sling for 24 hours

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse emphasize to prevent lead dislodgement during the first several weeks after pacemaker placement?

options.text: Avoid raising the left elbow above shoulder level or lifting more than 5 to 10 pounds
Keep the left arm completely immobilized in a sling for 6 weeks
Avoid using household microwave ovens within 10 feet of the chest
Perform overhead arm-stretching exercises three times daily starting tomorrow

rationales.summary: Limiting abduction and overhead movement on the affected side prevents mechanical traction and dislodgement of newly implanted endocardial leads.
rationales.A: Correct. Avoiding raising the arm above shoulder height and avoiding heavy lifting for 4-6 weeks allows lead tips to endothelialize securely.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Prolonged complete immobilization causes adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder); gentle below-shoulder movement is encouraged after 24-48 hours.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Modern pacemakers are shielded against properly functioning household microwaves.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Overhead stretching in the immediate postoperative period risks lead dislodgement.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 71-year-old male admitted for observation of a known 5.8 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) awaiting endovascular repair.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Suddenly reports severe, tearing lower back and flank pain; skin is pale, cool, and clammy.

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Notify the vascular surgeon immediately while ensuring two large-bore IV lines are patent
Palpate the abdomen deeply to assess for an expanding pulsatile mass
Administer the scheduled oral metoprolol to lower heart rate
Infuse 2 liters of warm normal saline rapidly to normalize blood pressure to 140/80 mmHg

rationales.summary: Sudden tearing back/flank pain with hypotension and tachycardia indicates impending or active AAA rupture requiring immediate surgical intervention.
rationales.A: Correct. Ruptured AAA is a surgical emergency; immediate surgeon notification and large-bore IV access for blood product resuscitation are top priorities.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Deep abdominal palpation is strictly contraindicated as mechanical pressure can precipitate catastrophic free rupture.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Administering a beta-blocker during hemorrhagic shock worsens hypotension and is unsafe in an NPO surgical candidate.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Aggressive crystalloid resuscitation to normotension ('popping the clot') worsens hemorrhage; permissive hypotension until surgical control is standard.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 64-year-old male in the CCU 18 hours after an extensive anterior wall myocardial infarction.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lethargic, cool mottled extremities, bilateral crackles halfway up lung fields, JVD present, urine output 12 mL over the past hour.
provider_orders: Titrate vasoactive drips per CCU protocol

questions.stem: Complete the bowtie by identifying the most likely condition, two priority nursing/medical interventions, and two parameters to monitor.

actions: Initiate dobutamine and norepinephrine infusions as prescribed
Administer supplemental high-flow oxygen or prepare for noninvasive ventilation
Infuse 3,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 hour
Administer IV furosemide 80 mg push before stabilizing blood pressure
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
parameters: Hourly urine output and serum lactate levels
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) and lung sounds

actions: Initiate dobutamine and norepinephrine infusions as prescribed
Administer supplemental high-flow oxygen or prepare for noninvasive ventilation
parameters: Hourly urine output and serum lactate levels
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) and lung sounds

rationales.summary: Post-MI pump failure with hypotension, pulmonary edema, JVD, and oliguria defines cardiogenic shock requiring inotropic/vasopressor support and oxygenation.
rationales.condition: Cardiogenic shock is evidenced by LVEF 20%, pulmonary crackles, JVD, hypotension, and end-organ hypoperfusion (oliguria, elevated lactate).
rationales.actions: Inotropes (dobutamine) and vasopressors (norepinephrine) restore contractility and coronary perfusion pressure, while supplemental oxygen corrects hypoxemia. Large fluid boluses worsen pulmonary edema, and IV diuretics before BP support worsen hypotension.
rationales.parameters: Hourly urine output (>=30 mL/hr), lactate clearance, MAP (>=65 mmHg), and pulmonary crackles track tissue perfusion and fluid tolerance.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 81-year-old female taking digoxin and furosemide for heart failure and atrial fibrillation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports nausea, anorexia, and yellow-green halos around ceiling lights.

diagnostic_results.ECG: Sinus bradycardia with frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)

provider_orders: Draw STAT electrolytes and digoxin level

questions.stem: Which electrolyte abnormality contributed most directly to this client's digoxin toxicity?

options.text: Hypokalemia
Hypernatremia
Hypocalcemia
Hyperphosphatemia

rationales.summary: Hypokalemia enhances digoxin binding to myocardial Na+/K+-ATPase pumps, precipitating toxicity even at borderline serum concentrations.
rationales.A: Correct. Potassium competes with digoxin for binding sites on Na+/K+-ATPase; loop diuretic-induced hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L) markedly increases digoxin toxicity.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Hypernatremia does not directly potentiate digoxin binding.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hypercalcemia (not hypocalcemia) increases intracellular calcium and worsens digoxin-induced arrhythmias.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Hyperphosphatemia is not a primary trigger of digoxin toxicity.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 57-year-old male returned to the step-down unit 30 minutes ago following right femoral artery coronary angiography with stent placement.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Nurse enters the room for routine post-procedure checks and observes bright red blood pooling beneath the client's right groin dressing.

diagnostic_results.Procedure note: 6-French right femoral arterial sheath removed with manual compression

medications: Clopidogrel 600 mg loading dose given in cath lab
provider_orders: Bed rest with right leg straight for 6 hours

questions.stem: Place the nurse's actions in the correct order of priority from first to last.

items: Don sterile gloves and apply firm manual pressure 1 to 2 cm above the percutaneous puncture site
Activate the call light to summon assistance and have another nurse notify the interventional cardiologist
Assess vital signs and right dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses while maintaining continuous pressure
Apply a sterile pressure dressing once hemostasis is achieved and document blood loss and neurovascular status

correct_response: Don sterile gloves and apply firm manual pressure 1 to 2 cm above the percutaneous puncture site
Activate the call light to summon assistance and have another nurse notify the interventional cardiologist
Assess vital signs and right dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses while maintaining continuous pressure
Apply a sterile pressure dressing once hemostasis is achieved and document blood loss and neurovascular status

rationales.summary: Active arterial hemorrhage requires immediate direct manual pressure slightly proximal to the skin entry site (where the artery was punctured) before calling for help.
rationales.1: Direct pressure 1-2 cm above the skin puncture site compresses the actual arterial arteriotomy and stops hemorrhage immediately.
rationales.2: Summoning help without leaving the bedside ensures continuous hemostatic pressure while alerting the provider.
rationales.3: Assessing hemodynamics and distal perfusion verifies systemic stability and limb viability during compression.
rationales.4: Securing a pressure dressing and documenting completes post-event stabilization.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 63-year-old female 1 day post-total hip arthroplasty.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, surgical hip dressing dry, mild bilateral lower extremity trace edema.
provider_orders: Sequential compression devices (SCDs) while in bed

questions.stem: Which nursing action is essential when administering enoxaparin to this client?

options.text: Inject into the anterolateral abdominal wall without expelling the air bubble from the prefilled syringe
Aspirate gently after needle insertion and massage the site for 1 minute afterward
Administer the injection intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle
Expel the nitrogen air bubble before injecting to prevent tissue necrosis

rationales.summary: Prefilled low-molecular-weight heparin syringes contain a calibrated air lock that clears the needle hub and prevents subcutaneous bruising.
rationales.A: Correct. Injecting into the love-handle area (at least 2 inches from the umbilicus) with the air bubble intact ensures full dose delivery and reduces bruising.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Aspirating and massaging after subcutaneous heparin/enoxaparin causes capillary trauma and hematoma formation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Enoxaparin is given strictly subcutaneously, never intramuscularly.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Expelling the air bubble results in medication loss and surface tracking.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 34-year-old male admitted with sharp, pleuritic substernal chest pain following a viral upper respiratory infection.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Pain worsens when lying flat and improves when sitting upright and leaning forward; high-pitched scratchy sound heard at left sternal border.

diagnostic_results.12-lead ECG: Diffuse concave upward ST-segment elevation across most leads with PR-segment depression

medications: Ibuprofen 600 mg PO every 8 hours with food
provider_orders: Echocardiogram to evaluate for pericardial effusion

questions.stem: Which complication should the nurse monitor for most closely in this client?

options.text: Pericardial effusion progressing to cardiac tamponade
Acute mitral valve papillary muscle rupture
Ascending thoracic aortic dissection
Pulmonary arterial embolism

rationales.summary: Pericardial inflammation causes fluid accumulation within the pericardial sac, which can compress the heart chambers and lead to cardiac tamponade.
rationales.A: Correct. Acute pericarditis can produce a rapidly accumulating pericardial effusion resulting in life-threatening cardiac tamponade.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Papillary muscle rupture is a mechanical complication of acute myocardial infarction, not viral pericarditis.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Aortic dissection is associated with severe hypertension or connective tissue disorders.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Pulmonary embolism is unrelated to viral pericardial inflammation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 68-year-old male admitted with an acute exacerbation of severe COPD.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Using accessory neck muscles, prolonged expiratory phase with diffuse expiratory wheezes, barrel chest.

laboratory_results.ABG: pH 7.31, PaCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 29 mEq/L, PaO2 52 mmHg

diagnostic_results.Chest X-ray: Hyperinflated lung fields, flattened diaphragms, no focal infiltrate

provider_orders: Titrate supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 88% to 92%

questions.stem: Which oxygen delivery device is most appropriate for achieving the prescribed target saturation in this client?

options.text: Venturi mask set at 28% FiO2
Non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
Simple face mask at 10 L/min
Nasal cannula at 6 L/min

rationales.summary: A Venturi mask delivers a precise, fixed FiO2 regardless of the client's breathing pattern, preventing hyperoxia-induced hypercapnia in COPD.
rationales.A: Correct. The Venturi mask provides exact FiO2 control (e.g., 24%-28%) to safely maintain SpO2 at 88%-92%.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delivering ~90%-100% FiO2 via non-rebreather worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch and Haldane effect, aggravating hypercapnic acidosis.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Simple face masks deliver variable high FiO2 (40%-60%) and risk CO2 retention if flow is too low.
rationales.D: Incorrect. High nasal cannula flow rates deliver unpredictable FiO2 depending on minute ventilation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 44-year-old male with a right-sided chest tube connected to a wet-suction water-seal drainage system for a spontaneous pneumothorax.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild incisional pain at insertion site, diminished right breath sounds at base, trachea midline.
medications: Morphine 2 mg IV every 3 hours PRN pain
provider_orders: Chest tube to -20 cm H2O suction
Keep sterile petroleum gauze and hemostats at bedside

questions.stem: Which findings in the chest tube drainage system require immediate nursing intervention? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continuous vigorous bubbling in the water-seal chamber
Gentle fluctuation (tidaling) of fluid in the water-seal chamber during respiration
Bright red drainage of 250 mL in the collection chamber over 1 hour
Chest tube accidentally disconnects from the drainage tubing
Drainage collection unit placed on the floor below chest level

rationales.summary: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber indicates an air leak, brisk bloody output signals hemorrhage, and tubing disconnection risks open pneumothorax.
rationales.A: Correct. Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber (unlike the suction control chamber) indicates an air leak in the system or pleural space.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Tidaling with inhalation and exhalation is a normal expected finding showing system patency.
rationales.C: Correct. Drainage exceeding 100-150 mL/hr (250 mL/hr) indicates active intrathoracic hemorrhage requiring urgent provider notification.
rationales.D: Correct. Disconnection exposes the pleural space to atmospheric air; the tube tip should immediately be submerged in sterile water while reconnecting.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Keeping the unit below chest level is standard practice to prevent retrograde fluid entry.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 47-year-old female 3 days post-pelvic surgery who suddenly develops acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Tachypneic, anxious, clear lung sounds on auscultation, right calf swollen and tender.

diagnostic_results.CT Pulmonary Angiogram: Large bilateral saddle pulmonary emboli with right ventricular strain

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse perform first?

options.text: Apply high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask and elevate the head of the bed
Administer the initial intravenous bolus of unfractionated heparin
Insert a Foley catheter to monitor hourly urine output
Obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram

rationales.summary: Using the Airway-Breathing-Circulation framework, correcting severe acute hypoxemia (SpO2 86%) takes immediate precedence before anticoagulation.
rationales.A: Correct. Oxygenation and upright positioning immediately improve alveolar oxygen tension and reduce pulmonary vasoconstriction.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Anticoagulation is critical immediately after oxygenation, as it prevents clot propagation rather than immediately reversing hypoxemia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Urine output monitoring is secondary to oxygenation and anticoagulation.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Obtaining an ECG should not delay oxygen delivery.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 53-year-old male mechanically ventilated in the ICU for severe ARDS secondary to urosepsis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sedated (RASS -3), coarse bilateral crackles throughout all lung fields.

laboratory_results.ABG: pH 7.29, PaCO2 50 mmHg, PaO2 54 mmHg (PaO2/FiO2 ratio = 67.5)

provider_orders: Low tidal volume lung-protective ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW)
Initiate prone positioning protocol for 16 hours/day

questions.stem: What is the primary physiological mechanism by which prone positioning improves oxygenation in severe ARDS?

options.text: It recruits collapsed dorsal alveoli and promotes more uniform ventilation-perfusion matching
It increases peak inspiratory airway pressures to force fluid out of the alveoli
It reduces left ventricular afterload by compressing the abdominal aorta
It stimulates endogenous surfactant synthesis within 30 minutes

rationales.summary: Prone positioning relieves dorsal lung compression caused by the heart and abdominal contents, recruiting dependent alveoli and homogenizing V/Q matching.
rationales.A: Correct. In supine patients, dependent dorsal lung regions collapse under the weight of the heart and mediastinum; proning opens dorsal alveoli while perfusion remains well distributed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. High peak pressures cause barotrauma and volutrauma, which lung-protective ARDS care actively avoids.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Prone positioning does not work via aortic compression.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Proning is a mechanical recruitment strategy, not a rapid surfactant stimulant.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 27-year-old female with moderate persistent asthma attending an outpatient follow-up visit.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lungs clear on auscultation, speaks in full sentences, using rescue inhaler 4 times per week.
medications: Fluticasone propionate HFA 2 puffs twice daily
Albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4-6 hours PRN
provider_orders: Review inhaler technique and asthma action plan

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse emphasize to prevent a common local adverse effect of fluticasone propionate?

options.text: Rinse the mouth with water and spit it out after each inhalation
Inhale the medication rapidly before using the albuterol inhaler
Use the fluticasone inhaler only when experiencing acute wheezing
Swallow a full glass of milk immediately after using the inhaler

rationales.summary: Inhaled corticosteroids deposit on the oropharyngeal mucosa, predisposing clients to oral candidiasis (thrush) and dysphonia unless rinsed out.
rationales.A: Correct. Rinsing and spitting removes residual corticosteroid from the oral mucosa and prevents oropharyngeal candidiasis.
rationales.B: Incorrect. When both are used together, the bronchodilator (albuterol) is administered first to open airways, and MDI inhalations should be slow and deep.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Fluticasone is a maintenance anti-inflammatory controller medication, not a rescue bronchodilator.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Swallowing milk does not clear mucosal steroid residue as effectively as rinsing and spitting.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 62-year-old male 48 hours post-surgical tracheostomy placement for laryngeal carcinoma.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Suddenly begins coughing forcefully during repositioning, dislodging the entire tracheostomy tube onto his chest.

diagnostic_results.Airway note: Fresh tracheostomy tract (<72 hours old); stay sutures present

provider_orders: Keep spare tracheostomy tube (same size and one size smaller) and obturator at bedside

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take immediately?

options.text: Call for emergency assistance, pull the stay sutures to open the stoma, and insert the spare tracheostomy tube with obturator
Cover the neck stoma with an occlusive dressing and perform a jaw-thrust maneuver
Attempt to force the dislodged, uncleaned tracheostomy tube back in without an obturator
Administer 100% oxygen via nasal cannula while waiting for the surgeon to arrive

rationales.summary: Accidental decannulation within the first 72 hours is an airway emergency because the stomal tract is immature and can close rapidly.
rationales.A: Correct. Summoning emergency airway support while gently retracting stay sutures and inserting the sterile spare tube with obturator (removing the obturator immediately after entry) restores the airway.
rationales.B: Incorrect. An occlusive dressing blocks the surgical airway in a client with laryngeal obstruction.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Reinserting without an obturator risks creating a false tract in the pretracheal tissue.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nasal cannula oxygen cannot bypass a laryngeal tumor when the stoma is closing.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 41-year-old male admitted with a 4-week history of productive cough, hemoptysis, fever, and 15-pound unintentional weight loss.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Cachectic, coarse crackles in right upper lobe.
provider_orders: Baseline liver function tests and visual acuity exam

questions.stem: Which infection control measures must the nurse implement for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room with the door kept closed
Wear a fit-tested N95 or higher-level particulate respirator upon entering the room
Place a surgical mask on the client if transport out of the room is medically necessary
Wear a standard surgical mask when standing within 3 feet of the client
Explain that RIPE medications may turn body fluids reddish-orange and require periodic liver monitoring

rationales.summary: Active pulmonary tuberculosis requires airborne precautions (negative-pressure room, N95 respirator for staff, surgical mask on client during transport) and RIPE hepatotoxicity/adverse effect teaching.
rationales.A: Correct. Negative-pressure ventilation (6-12 air changes/hr) prevents droplet nuclei from escaping into corridors.
rationales.B: Correct. Staff must wear fit-tested N95 respirators to filter airborne Mycobacterium tuberculosis droplet nuclei.
rationales.C: Correct. A surgical mask worn by the client contains respiratory secretions during essential transport.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Standard surgical masks are for droplet precautions, not airborne precautions.
rationales.E: Correct. Rifampin causes harmless orange-red discoloration of urine/tears/sweat, and INH/rifampin/pyrazinamide carry hepatotoxicity risk.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 66-year-old female mechanically ventilated via an endotracheal tube for pneumonia-induced respiratory failure.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Restless, biting on the oral endotracheal tube, coarse rhonchi present; high-pressure ventilator alarm sounds continuously.

diagnostic_results.Chest X-ray: ET tube tip 3.5 cm above carina; right lower lobe infiltrate

provider_orders: Volume-assist control ventilation, Vt 420 mL, PEEP 8 cm H2O

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first to resolve the high-pressure ventilator alarm?

options.text: Assess the client's airway, suction secretions, and insert a bite block if needed
Check the ventilator circuit for a disconnected tube or deflated ET tube cuff
Silence the alarm and increase the high-pressure limit setting
Extubate the client immediately and initiate bag-valve-mask ventilation

rationales.summary: High-pressure ventilator alarms indicate increased airway resistance or decreased lung compliance (secretions, biting tube, kinked tubing, bronchospasm, pneumothorax).
rationales.A: Correct. Assessing the client first—clearing secretions via suctioning and preventing tube biting—directly addresses the most common causes of high peak airway pressure.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Circuit disconnection or cuff leak causes a low-pressure alarm, not a high-pressure alarm.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Raising alarm limits masks airway obstruction and risks barotrauma.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Unplanned extubation removes a secure airway unnecessarily.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 84-year-old female brought from an assisted living facility with new-onset acute confusion and lethargy.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Disoriented to place and time (baseline alert and oriented x4), bronchial breath sounds and egophony in left lower lung field.
provider_orders: Incentive spirometry every hour while awake

questions.stem: Which finding is most characteristic of atypical presentation of pneumonia in older adults?

options.text: Acute confusion and tachypnea without a high fever
High spiking fever above 40 C with rigors
Bradycardia and hypertension
Generalized urticarial rash

rationales.summary: Older adults frequently present with blunted febrile responses and exhibit acute delirium/confusion and tachypnea as early signs of pneumonia.
rationales.A: Correct. Acute mental status change and elevated respiratory rate (>24 breaths/min) are often the earliest indicators of infection in geriatric clients even when afebrile.
rationales.B: Incorrect. High spiking fevers are more typical in younger adults.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Tachycardia and borderline hypotension occur rather than bradycardia and hypertension.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Rash is not a typical presentation of bacterial pneumonia.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 59-year-old male undergoing bedside ultrasound-guided right thoracentesis for a large malignant pleural effusion.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sitting upright leaning over an overbed table; 1,100 mL of serosanguinous fluid drained so far.
provider_orders: Limit fluid removal to <= 1,000-1,500 mL per session

questions.stem: The client suddenly begins coughing incessantly and reports chest tightness during fluid removal. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Alert the provider immediately to stop fluid withdrawal and assess for re-expansion pulmonary edema or pneumothorax
Encourage the client to take deep breaths and continue draining until the effusion is completely empty
Place the client flat in the supine position immediately
Administer an oral antitussive cough syrup

rationales.summary: Incessant coughing, chest tightness, or hypotension after removing >1,000 mL of pleural fluid signals re-expansion pulmonary edema or pneumothorax.
rationales.A: Correct. Rapid removal of large effusion volumes can trigger re-expansion pulmonary edema or mediastinal shift; drainage must be stopped immediately.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Continuing drainage worsens re-expansion pulmonary edema.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Supine positioning impairs ventilation in a dyspneic patient.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Masking the cough with antitussives ignores a serious mechanical/pulmonary complication.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 23-year-old male with cystic fibrosis admitted for an acute pulmonary exacerbation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Digital clubbing, productive cough with thick tenacious green sputum, scattered rhonchi, BMI 18.2 kg/m2.

diagnostic_results.Chest CT: Bilateral upper-lobe bronchiectasis and mucus plugging

provider_orders: High-frequency chest wall oscillation vest twice daily

questions.stem: Which nursing interventions are appropriate for managing this client's respiratory and nutritional needs? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administer albuterol nebulizer before chest physiotherapy to maximize airway clearance
Administer pancrelipase capsules immediately before every meal and snack
Perform chest physiotherapy immediately after lunch to prevent fatigue
Provide fat-soluble vitamin supplements (A, D, E, K) as prescribed
Restrict sodium and fluid intake to thin respiratory secretions

rationales.summary: Cystic fibrosis care requires bronchodilation prior to airway clearance, pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals/snacks, and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.
rationales.A: Correct. Bronchodilators open airways prior to airway clearance techniques.
rationales.B: Correct. Pancreatic enzymes must be taken with all meals and snacks to digest fats, proteins, and carbohydrates.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Chest physiotherapy should be performed at least 1-2 hours after meals to prevent vomiting and aspiration.
rationales.D: Correct. Pancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Liberal fluids are needed to hydrate secretions, and CF clients lose excess sodium in sweat.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 22-year-old female in the emergency department with severe asthma exacerbation refractory to three consecutive albuterol/ipratropium nebulizers.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sitting upright unable to speak single words, markedly decreased breath sounds with absent wheezing ('silent chest'), diaphoretic.

questions.stem: How should the nurse interpret the sudden disappearance of wheezing alongside a rising PaCO2 of 52 mmHg?

options.text: Impending respiratory arrest due to critical airflow obstruction and ventilatory muscle fatigue
Rapid resolution of bronchospasm following nebulizer and magnesium therapy
Expected therapeutic hyperventilation response to methylprednisolone
Development of a spontaneous tension pneumothorax

rationales.summary: In severe asthma, a 'silent chest' and normal-to-elevated PaCO2 indicate minimal air movement and exhausting respiratory muscles requiring emergent intubation.
rationales.A: Correct. Wheezing requires airflow; when airflow drops to near zero ('silent chest') and PaCO2 rises from hypocapnia into hypercapnia, respiratory arrest is imminent.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Clinical improvement would be accompanied by improved air entry, speaking in phrases, and falling respiratory rate.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2; a rising PaCO2 indicates hypoventilation.
rationales.D: Incorrect. While pneumothorax can occur, bilateral silent chest with hypercapnia specifically reflects end-stage status asthmaticus.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 54-year-old male admitted for laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a documented history of severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: BMI 36 kg/m2, neck circumference 18 inches, uses CPAP at 12 cm H2O nightly at home.
medications: Hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV every 3 hours PRN severe pain
provider_orders: Use home CPAP machine during all sleep periods

questions.stem: Which postoperative nursing measure is highest priority to prevent airway obstruction and respiratory depression in this client?

options.text: Apply the client's CPAP device during sleep and use multimodal non-opioid analgesia to minimize opioid sedation
Position the client completely flat on his back to keep the cervical spine aligned
Administer a bedtime benzodiazepine to ensure uninterrupted postoperative sleep
Turn off pulse oximetry alarms at night so the client is not awakened

rationales.summary: Clients with OSA are highly sensitive to opioid-induced pharyngeal collapse and respiratory depression; CPAP and opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia protect airway patency.
rationales.A: Correct. Positive airway pressure splints the upper airway open, and minimizing opioids reduces central respiratory depression.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Supine positioning allows the tongue and soft palate to fall posteriorly, worsening airway collapse; lateral or semi-Fowler positioning is preferred.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Sedative-hypnotics exacerbate upper airway relaxation and apnea.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Continuous oximetry/capnography monitoring is critical for detecting nocturnal desaturation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 48-year-old female with a 25-pack-year smoking history starting transdermal nicotine patch therapy (21 mg/24 hr).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Motivated to quit smoking, mild morning smoker's cough, lungs clear.

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse include when teaching the client how to use the transdermal nicotine patch safely?

options.text: Apply a new patch daily to a clean, dry, hairless skin site and rotate sites to prevent irritation
Continue smoking 3 to 4 cigarettes daily during the first two weeks to prevent withdrawal
Cut the 21 mg patch in half if vivid dreams occur
Apply the patch over the same area of the upper arm every day for consistent absorption

rationales.summary: Rotating clean, hairless application sites daily minimizes localized erythema and ensures steady transdermal nicotine absorption.
rationales.A: Correct. Rotating sites daily (waiting at least 7 days before reusing a site) prevents contact dermatitis.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Smoking while wearing a nicotine patch risks acute nicotine toxicity (tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Cutting matrix/reservoir patches can alter drug release kinetics; removing the patch at bedtime (if using a 16-hr schedule) or stepping down doses should be discussed with the provider.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Reusing the same site daily causes local skin irritation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 65-year-old male brought to the emergency department 55 minutes after sudden onset of right-sided hemiplegia and expressive aphasia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score 14, alert, unable to lift right arm or leg.

diagnostic_results.Non-contrast Head CT: No intracranial hemorrhage or mass effect

provider_orders: Prepare for intravenous tenecteplase (TNK) thrombolytic therapy
Lower blood pressure to < 185/110 mmHg prior to thrombolysis

questions.stem: Which medication should the nurse prepare to administer first to safely qualify this client for intravenous thrombolytic therapy?

options.text: Labetalol 10 to 20 mg intravenously
Aspirin 325 mg orally
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg
Heparin 5,000 units intravenously

rationales.summary: Blood pressure must be gently lowered below 185/110 mmHg using IV labetalol or nicardipine before administering thrombolytics to prevent hemorrhagic transformation.
rationales.A: Correct. IV labetalol (or nicardipine) allows controlled BP reduction to <185/110 mmHg required before IV thrombolysis.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants are contraindicated for 24 hours after thrombolytic administration, and the client has not had a dysphagia screen.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Sublingual nifedipine causes precipitous, unpredictable hypotension that worsens cerebral penumbral ischemia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Heparin increases intracranial hemorrhage risk and is contraindicated with thrombolytics.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 39-year-old male in the neuro-ICU following a severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) with an intraventricular ICP monitor.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score 8 (E2 V2 M4), pupils 4 mm equal and sluggishly reactive.

diagnostic_results.ICP monitor: Sustained ICP 24 mmHg (normal 5-15 mmHg), CPP 80 mmHg

medications: Mannitol 0.5 g/kg IV PRN ICP > 20 mmHg

questions.stem: Which nursing interventions help reduce elevated intracranial pressure in this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain the head and neck in a neutral midline position
Administer antipyretics and cooling measures promptly to prevent fever
Cluster nursing care activities such as suctioning, bathing, and turning together
Pre-oxygenate with 100% oxygen and limit endotracheal suctioning to <= 10-15 seconds
Flex the client's hips sharply to 90 degrees to promote venous return

rationales.summary: ICP management relies on facilitating cerebral venous drainage (midline neck, 30-degree HOB), avoiding hyperthermia/hypoxia/hypercapnia, and spacing stimulating interventions.
rationales.A: Correct. Neutral midline neck alignment prevents jugular venous compression and promotes cerebral venous outflow.
rationales.B: Correct. Fever increases cerebral metabolic demand and cerebral blood flow, driving ICP higher.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Clustering multiple stimulating activities causes cumulative spikes in ICP; care should be spaced.
rationales.D: Correct. Pre-oxygenating and limiting suction duration prevents hypoxia and hypercapnia-induced cerebral vasodilation.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Extreme hip flexion increases intra-abdominal and intrathoracic pressure, impairing cerebral venous drainage.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 31-year-old male with a C6 complete spinal cord injury admitted for urinary tract infection treatment.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Suddenly reports a pounding headache; profuse diaphoresis and flushing noted above the clavicles, goosebumps and pallor below.

diagnostic_results.Bladder scan: 580 mL urine; indwelling Foley tubing found kinked beneath leg

questions.stem: Place the nurse's interventions in the correct priority sequence from first to last.

items: Elevate the head of the bed to 90 degrees (high Fowler position) and lower the legs
Loosen any tight clothing, abdominal binder, or anti-embolism stockings
Uncoiling/unkinking the Foley catheter tubing to drain the distended urinary bladder
Recheck blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes and administer prescribed antihypertensive therapy if BP remains elevated

correct_response: Elevate the head of the bed to 90 degrees (high Fowler position) and lower the legs
Loosen any tight clothing, abdominal binder, or anti-embolism stockings
Uncoiling/unkinking the Foley catheter tubing to drain the distended urinary bladder
Recheck blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes and administer prescribed antihypertensive therapy if BP remains elevated

rationales.summary: Autonomic dysreflexia (lesions at or above T6) causes life-threatening reflex hypertension; immediate orthostatic blood pooling via upright positioning precedes removing noxious stimuli.
rationales.1: Sitting the client upright at 90 degrees immediately uses orthostatic pooling in the lower extremities to lower cerebral blood pressure and prevent hemorrhagic stroke.
rationales.2: Loosening constrictive garments removes external cutaneous triggers and prevents blood pressure trapping.
rationales.3: Bladder distension is the #1 trigger of autonomic dysreflexia; unkinking the catheter resolves the noxious afferent stimulus.
rationales.4: Frequent BP monitoring and rapid-acting vasodilators are used if hypertension persists after removing the trigger.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 29-year-old female with epilepsy admitted after breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Client suddenly cries out, loses consciousness, and develops generalized tonic-clonic motor activity.
medications: Lorazepam 2 mg IV push PRN seizure > 5 minutes

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take during the active tonic-clonic phase of the seizure?

options.text: Turn the client onto her side, protect her head, loosen tight neck clothing, and note the exact start time
Insert a padded tongue blade between her teeth to prevent tongue biting
Restrain her upper and lower extremities firmly to prevent musculoskeletal fractures
Immediately insert a rigid Yankauer suction catheter into the back of the pharynx

rationales.summary: During an active seizure, airway protection via lateral positioning, injury prevention, and timing seizure duration (to identify status epilepticus at 5 minutes) are essential.
rationales.A: Correct. Side-lying positioning prevents aspiration of saliva, head padding prevents trauma, and timing determines when rescue benzodiazepines are indicated.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Forcing anything into the mouth during tonic jaw clenching breaks teeth and causes airway obstruction.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Restraining convulsing limbs increases the risk of fractures and soft-tissue injury.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Suctioning is performed after motor activity stops if secretions remain; forcing a rigid catheter into a clenched jaw causes trauma.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 45-year-old female with generalized myasthenia gravis admitted with worsening dysphagia, diplopia, and generalized weakness.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Weak cough, nasal speech, shallow respirations, uses accessory muscles.

diagnostic_results.Bedside Spirometry: Forced vital capacity (FVC) 11 mL/kg (decreased from 28 mL/kg)

medications: Pyridostigmine 60 mg PO every 4 hours while awake
provider_orders: Measure FVC and negative inspiratory force (NIF) every 2 hours
Hold oral medications if dysphagia worsens

questions.stem: Based on the client's forced vital capacity and respiratory status, which intervention is the immediate priority?

options.text: Prepare for emergent endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
Administer the scheduled dose of pyridostigmine with applesauce
Encourage deep breathing and incentive spirometry every hour
Administer lorazepam 1 mg IV to relieve respiratory anxiety

rationales.summary: An FVC < 15 mL/kg (client is at 11 mL/kg) with rising PaCO2 signals neuromuscular respiratory failure (myasthenic crisis) requiring elective intubation before arrest.
rationales.A: Correct. FVC < 15 mL/kg or NIF < -20 cm H2O indicates severe diaphragmatic weakness requiring immediate airway support.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Oral administration is unsafe with severe dysphagia and weak cough (aspiration risk), and pyridostigmine is often temporarily held during mechanical ventilation in myasthenic crisis to reduce secretions.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Incentive spirometry cannot reverse diaphragmatic neuromuscular failure.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Benzodiazepines suppress central respiratory drive and worsen neuromuscular hypoventilation.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 38-year-old male admitted 2 weeks after Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis with symmetric ascending lower-extremity weakness and paresthesias.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Absent patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes, 2/5 strength in lower extremities, 4/5 strength in upper extremities.

laboratory_results.CSF analysis: Albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein 112 mg/dL, normal WBC 2/mm3)

questions.stem: Which assessment finding indicates that the demyelination is progressing to a life-threatening stage?

options.text: Weak cough, inability to count to 15 in a single breath, and declining vital capacity
Tingling sensations in the soles of both feet
Absent ankle jerk reflexes
Mild aching pain in the lumbar paraspinal muscles

rationales.summary: Ascending paralysis in Guillain-Barre syndrome can rapidly involve the phrenic and intercostal nerves, causing acute respiratory failure.
rationales.A: Correct. Inability to count to 15-20 on one breath, weak cough, and falling vital capacity indicate diaphragmatic involvement requiring urgent ventilatory preparation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Distal paresthesias are an early baseline symptom.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Areflexia in the lower extremities is a standard diagnostic feature.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Neuropathic back/leg pain is common and not immediately life-threatening.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 73-year-old male with Parkinson disease admitted for a minor urologic procedure.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Resting pill-rolling tremor of right hand, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, shuffling gait.
provider_orders: Administer Parkinson medications strictly on home schedule

questions.stem: Which nursing intervention is most important when administering carbidopa-levodopa to this client?

options.text: Administer each dose at the exact scheduled time and avoid giving it with high-protein meals
Hold the morning dose until physical therapy has been completed
Administer the medication with a high-protein nutritional shake to enhance absorption
Discontinue the drug abruptly if orthostatic dizziness develops

rationales.summary: Carbidopa-levodopa has a short half-life requiring precise timing to prevent 'off' akinesia, and large neutral amino acids compete with levodopa transport across the gut and blood-brain barrier.
rationales.A: Correct. Exact dosing times prevent severe motor freezing, and separating doses from high-protein meals avoids amino acid competition for absorption.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delaying doses impairs mobility and increases fall risk during physical therapy.
rationales.C: Incorrect. High-protein shakes impair levodopa absorption.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy can precipitate neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome (parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome).

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 20-year-old college student brought to the emergency department with severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and fever.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, petechial rash on lower extremities, drowsy.
provider_orders: STAT blood cultures followed by empiric IV antibiotics

questions.stem: Which type of isolation precautions should the nurse initiate immediately upon suspicion of bacterial meningitis?

options.text: Droplet precautions until the client has received 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy
Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room for 14 days
Contact precautions only, using gown and gloves
Standard precautions only until CSF culture confirms Neisseria meningitidis

rationales.summary: Suspected bacterial meningitis (especially Neisseria meningitidis, suggested by petechiae) requires immediate droplet precautions until 24 hours after starting effective antimicrobials.
rationales.A: Correct. Droplet precautions (surgical mask within 3-6 feet, private room) are instituted immediately and maintained for the first 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Meningococcal organisms spread via large respiratory droplets, not airborne nuclei.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Contact precautions alone do not protect mucosal surfaces from respiratory droplets.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Waiting for culture confirmation exposes staff and visitors to transmissible meningococcal infection.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 51-year-old female in the neuro-ICU day 5 following endovascular coiling of a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Previously alert and oriented, now becomes lethargic with new left arm drift.

diagnostic_results.Transcranial Doppler: Elevated mean flow velocity in right middle cerebral artery

medications: Nimodipine 60 mg via NG tube every 4 hours

questions.stem: What is the primary therapeutic purpose of administering nimodipine to this client?

options.text: To prevent and minimize delayed cerebral ischemia caused by cerebral vasospasm
To dissolve residual subarachnoid blood clots in the basal cisterns
To prevent post-aneurysmal generalized tonic-clonic seizures
To aggressively lower systemic systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg

rationales.summary: Cerebral vasospasm peaks 4 to 14 days after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage; nimodipine (a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) improves neurological outcomes from vasospasm.
rationales.A: Correct. Nimodipine selectively crosses the blood-brain barrier to reduce ischemic neurological deficits associated with cerebral vasospasm.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Nimodipine is not a thrombolytic agent.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Antiseizure medications (e.g., levetiracetam), not calcium channel blockers, prevent seizures.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Dropping systolic BP below 100 mmHg during vasospasm would worsen cerebral ischemia.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 82-year-old male with moderate Alzheimer disease admitted to a medical unit for cellulitis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Becomes increasingly agitated and disoriented at 1830, attempting to climb out of bed looking for his car keys.

questions.stem: Which nursing approach is most therapeutic for managing this client's sundowning agitation?

options.text: Acknowledge his feelings calmly, redirect him to a familiar activity, and maintain a well-lit, quiet environment
Firmly argue with him that he sold his car five years ago and is in a hospital
Apply bilateral wrist restraints immediately to prevent him from leaving the bed
Turn off all room lights at 1830 so he will go to sleep early

rationales.summary: Validation, calm redirection, adequate evening lighting to reduce shadows, and minimizing overstimulation effectively de-escalate sundowning behaviors.
rationales.A: Correct. Validating emotion without confrontation and redirecting while reducing visual shadows lowers evening confusion and agitation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Confrontation and logical arguing escalate frustration and fear in moderate dementia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Physical restraints worsen agitation, increase injury risk, and are a last resort.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Dim lighting creates frightening shadows that exacerbate sundowning.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 35-year-old female with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS) discharged after IV methylprednisolone therapy for an acute optic neuritis flare.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Visual acuity improving, mild lower extremity spasticity, reports chronic afternoon fatigue.
medications: Baclofen 10 mg PO three times daily

questions.stem: Which self-management strategies should the nurse include in the client's discharge teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid hot baths, saunas, and overheating, which can temporarily worsen neurologic symptoms
Schedule demanding activities and exercise during the cooler morning hours with planned rest periods
Use a timed voiding schedule and adequate fluid intake to manage neurogenic bladder symptoms
Perform vigorous aerobic exercise to the point of exhaustion daily to build muscle strength
Stop taking baclofen abruptly once leg stiffness improves

rationales.summary: Heat sensitivity (Uhthoff phenomenon), energy conservation, and bladder retraining are cornerstones of multiple sclerosis self-management.
rationales.A: Correct. Elevated core body temperature slows conduction across demyelinated axons (Uhthoff phenomenon), exacerbating weakness and vision changes.
rationales.B: Correct. Morning pacing with scheduled rest combats MS-related fatigue.
rationales.C: Correct. Scheduled voiding prevents urinary retention, incontinence, and UTIs.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Exercising to exhaustion induces overheating and prolonged fatigue.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Abrupt baclofen withdrawal can cause severe rebound spasticity, hallucinations, and seizures.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 42-year-old female who underwent a diagnostic lumbar puncture 2 hours ago.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert and oriented, puncture dressing clean and dry, reports a new throbbing frontal headache that intensifies when sitting up and improves when lying flat.
medications: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN

questions.stem: Which nursing action is most appropriate to relieve this client's post-lumbar puncture headache?

options.text: Place the client in a flat supine position and encourage oral or intravenous hydration
Elevate the head of the bed to 60 degrees to reduce intracranial venous pressure
Restrict fluid intake to 1,000 mL/day to decrease cerebrospinal fluid production
Ambulate the client in the hallway to stimulate circulation

rationales.summary: Post-dural puncture headache results from CSF leakage through the dural defect causing downward traction on pain-sensitive meningeal structures when upright.
rationales.A: Correct. Supine positioning eliminates hydrostatic pressure across the dural puncture site, and hydration supports CSF replenishment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Elevating the head increases CSF leakage and worsens orthostatic post-LP headache.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Fluid restriction delays CSF volume restoration.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Upright ambulation exacerbates the headache.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 24-year-old female with type 1 diabetes mellitus admitted to the ICU step-down unit with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath odor.
medications: Regular insulin IV infusion ordered at 0.1 units/kg/hr
provider_orders: DKA protocol: IV fluids, potassium replacement, regular insulin infusion

questions.stem: Which action must the nurse take before initiating the continuous intravenous regular insulin infusion?

options.text: Hold the insulin infusion and administer prescribed IV potassium replacement until serum potassium is >= 3.3 mEq/L
Administer an IV bolus of sodium bicarbonate to correct the pH of 7.16
Start the insulin infusion immediately at double the ordered rate to rapidly drop glucose
Add 5% dextrose to the initial liter of normal saline

rationales.summary: Insulin drives extracellular potassium into cells; starting IV insulin when serum potassium is < 3.3 mEq/L can trigger fatal hypokalemic cardiac dysrhythmias.
rationales.A: Correct. Per ADA DKA guidelines, IV fluids and potassium replacement must precede insulin therapy whenever serum potassium is < 3.3 mEq/L.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate is generally avoided unless pH is < 6.9 because it worsens hypokalemia and paradoxical CNS acidosis.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Starting insulin at K+ 3.1 mEq/L risks ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Dextrose is added once blood glucose falls to ~200-250 mg/dL so insulin can continue clearing ketones without causing hypoglycemia.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 33-year-old female with untreated Graves disease admitted after a motor vehicle collision with acute thyroid storm.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Agitated, delirious, profuse diaphoresis, warm flushed skin, palpable thyroid bruit.

diagnostic_results.ECG: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

provider_orders: Administer PTU 1 hour prior to Lugol iodine solution

questions.stem: Why must propylthiouracil (PTU) be administered at least 1 hour before potassium iodide (Lugol solution)?

options.text: To block thyroid hormone synthesis first so the iodine load is not used as substrate to produce more thyroid hormone
Because Lugol solution causes severe gastritis unless neutralized by PTU
To prevent iodide-induced agranulocytosis and neutropenia
Because PTU chelates excess circulating thyroxine in the bloodstream

rationales.summary: Iodine inhibits preformed hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect), but if given before thioamides block organification, the hyperactive gland uses the iodine to synthesize new hormone.
rationales.A: Correct. Administering PTU (or methimazole) 1 hour beforehand blocks thyroid peroxidase synthesis before iodide inhibits hormone release.
rationales.B: Incorrect. PTU does not neutralize gastric acidity.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Agranulocytosis is a rare side effect of PTU/methimazole, not prevented by dosing order.
rationales.D: Incorrect. PTU inhibits new hormone synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion rather than chelating circulating hormone.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 44-year-old female with primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) brought to the emergency department after 2 days of viral gastroenteritis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Confused, severe generalized weakness, hyperpigmentation over knuckles and buccal mucosa, poor skin turgor.
medications: Hydrocortisone sodium succinate 100 mg IV push STAT

questions.stem: Which combination of electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities is classic for acute adrenal crisis?

options.text: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia
Hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia
Hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and metabolic alkalosis
Hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and hypercalcemia

rationales.summary: Deficiency of both aldosterone (sodium wasting, potassium retention) and cortisol (impaired gluconeogenesis and vascular tone) produces hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia.
rationales.A: Correct. Lack of aldosterone causes renal sodium loss and potassium retention, while lack of cortisol impairs gluconeogenesis and catecholamine sensitivity.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia characterize Cushing syndrome (cortisol/aldosterone excess).
rationales.C: Incorrect. These characterize primary hyperparathyroidism.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Potassium is elevated, not depleted, in primary adrenal insufficiency.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 60-year-old male with small-cell lung cancer admitted with worsening confusion and lethargy.
clinical_scenario.assessment: No peripheral edema, normal skin turgor, oriented to person only.

diagnostic_results.Head CT: Mild diffuse cerebral edema, no mass

medications: 3% Sodium Chloride IV infusion at 30 mL/hr

questions.stem: Why must the nurse monitor serum sodium every 2 hours so that correction does not exceed 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours?

options.text: Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS)
Hypertonic saline rapidly induces acute hyperkalemic cardiac arrest
Rapid sodium elevation triggers nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Serum sodium above 125 mEq/L precipitates acute pulmonary edema

rationales.summary: Brain cells adapt to chronic hyponatremia by shedding intracellular osmolytes; rapid serum sodium elevation shrinks oligodendrocytes and causes osmotic demyelination syndrome.
rationales.A: Correct. Raising serum sodium faster than 8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours causes irreversible pontine and extrapontine myelinolysis (dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Hypertonic saline does not cause hyperkalemic arrest.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Nephrogenic DI is not caused by sodium correction.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Careful rate control (30 mL/hr) prevents volume overload while protecting the brain.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 46-year-old female 6 hours post-total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild anterior neck swelling, reports tingling around her lips and fingertips.
medications: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV ordered PRN symptomatic hypocalcemia
provider_orders: Keep tracheostomy tray and suction at bedside

questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate in caring for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare to administer intravenous calcium gluconate as prescribed
Assess for inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and neck dressing tightness
Support the head and neck with pillows to avoid hyperextension of the suture line
Lower the head of the bed flat to reduce venous oozing at the surgical site
Monitor for carpopedal spasm (Trousseau sign) and laryngeal spasm

rationales.summary: Transient or permanent hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy causes acute hypocalcemia (circumoral paresthesias, positive Chvostek/Trousseau signs, laryngospasm) alongside airway hematoma risks.
rationales.A: Correct. Symptomatic post-thyroidectomy hypocalcemia requires IV calcium gluconate to prevent tetany and laryngospasm.
rationales.B: Correct. Stridor or neck tightness can signal expanding hematoma compressing the trachea or hypocalcemic laryngospasm.
rationales.C: Correct. Neutral neck support protects suture line integrity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Semi-Fowler positioning (30-45 degrees) reduces neck edema and venous pressure.
rationales.E: Correct. Neuromuscular irritability progresses from paresthesias to carpopedal and laryngeal spasm.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 49-year-old male 24 hours post-transsphenoidal hypophysectomy for a pituitary macroadenoma.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Intense thirst, dry skin, urine output 450 mL/hr for the past 3 consecutive hours, urine pale and watery.
medications: Desmopressin (DDAVP) 1 mcg IV PRN urine output > 250 mL/hr for 2 consecutive hours

questions.stem: Which nursing intervention is the highest priority for this client?

options.text: Administer the prescribed desmopressin (DDAVP) and replace fluid losses carefully
Restrict oral and intravenous fluid intake to 1,000 mL/day
Administer furosemide 20 mg IV to clear excess serum sodium
Pack both nostrils tightly with dry gauze to check for CSF leak

rationales.summary: Central diabetes insipidus following pituitary surgery causes massive free-water diuresis (specific gravity < 1.005) and hypernatremic dehydration requiring desmopressin and fluid replacement.
rationales.A: Correct. Desmopressin replaces deficient antidiuretic hormone to halt polyuria while hypotonic/balanced fluids correct the free-water deficit.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Restricting fluids in DI precipitates life-threatening hypernatremic hypovolemic shock.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Loop diuretics worsen free-water loss and hypernatremia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nasal packing is contraindicated post-transsphenoidal surgery; clear drainage should be tested for glucose/beta-2 transferrin without packing.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 67-year-old male admitted with oliguric acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Generalized muscle weakness, urine output 15 mL/hr (dark tea-colored).

diagnostic_results.12-lead ECG: Tall peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes

medications: Regular insulin 10 units IV with 50% dextrose 50 mL IV

questions.stem: Which prescribed medication should the nurse administer first to immediately protect the myocardium?

options.text: Calcium gluconate 10% intravenously
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate orally
Regular insulin 10 units intravenously with 50% dextrose
Albuterol 10 mg via nebulizer

rationales.summary: When hyperkalemia produces ECG conduction changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS), IV calcium gluconate antagonizes cardiac membrane excitability within 1 to 3 minutes.
rationales.A: Correct. Calcium gluconate stabilizes myocardial cell membranes immediately without altering serum potassium levels, buying time for shifting and removal therapies.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Gastrointestinal potassium binders take hours to remove potassium from the body.
rationales.C: Incorrect. IV insulin with dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly within 15-30 minutes and is given immediately after calcium membrane stabilization.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Beta-agonists shift potassium over 15-30 minutes and do not provide immediate membrane stabilization.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 63-year-old female with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) admitted for pneumonia; has a mature left forearm arteriovenous (AV) fistula.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Palpable vibration (thrill) and audible swishing sound (bruit) over left forearm fistula.
medications: Cefepime 1 g IV every 24 hours (renally dosed)
Sevelamer carbonate 800 mg PO with meals
provider_orders: Limb alert wristband on left arm

questions.stem: Which nursing measures are essential to protect the client's left arteriovenous fistula? Select all that apply.

options.text: Post signage and apply a limb-alert band prohibiting blood pressures and venipunctures on the left arm
Auscultate for a bruit and palpate for a thrill over the fistula every shift
Avoid tight dressings, watches, or sleeping on the left arm
Use the AV fistula for routine peripheral IV antibiotic infusions between dialysis sessions
Notify the provider immediately if the thrill or bruit disappears

rationales.summary: AV fistula preservation requires preventing external compression/trauma, prohibiting BP/venipuncture/routine IV access, and monitoring patency via thrill and bruit.
rationales.A: Correct. Cuff inflation and needle sticks can thrombose or rupture the high-flow vascular access.
rationales.B: Correct. Assessing both palpable thrill and audible bruit confirms continuous turbulent blood flow.
rationales.C: Correct. External constriction compromises fistula flow and promotes thrombosis.
rationales.D: Incorrect. AV fistulas are reserved exclusively for hemodialysis cannulation by trained dialysis staff.
rationales.E: Correct. Absence of a thrill/bruit indicates acute fistula thrombosis requiring urgent vascular intervention.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 55-year-old male performing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) admitted with abdominal pain and low-grade fever.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Diffuse abdominal tenderness with mild rebound, peritoneal dialysis effluent bag is cloudy.
provider_orders: Send peritoneal effluent for cell count, Gram stain, and culture

questions.stem: Which finding is the earliest and most cardinal indicator of peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis?

options.text: Cloudy peritoneal dialysate effluent
Blood-tinged effluent during the first exchange after catheter placement
Referred shoulder-tip pain during dialysate inflow
Slow outflow caused by fibrin strands in the tubing

rationales.summary: Cloudy dialysate effluent (due to elevated leukocytes and fibrin) is the earliest hallmark sign of peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis clients.
rationales.A: Correct. Peritonitis typically manifests first with cloudy outflow effluent, followed by abdominal pain and fever.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Pink or blood-tinged drainage is common in the first few exchanges after initial catheter insertion.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Shoulder-tip pain occurs from diaphragmatic irritation due to air or cold dialysate.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Fibrin strands can slow drainage mechanically without necessarily indicating infection.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 70-year-old male 4 hours post-transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) with a 3-way indwelling Foley catheter and continuous bladder irrigation (CBI).
