clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports severe lower abdominal bladder spasms and an intense urge to void; drainage tubing shows dark red fluid with clots and slow outflow.
medications: Belladonna and opium suppository PRN bladder spasms
provider_orders: Titrate CBI rate to maintain light pink to clear urine output

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the catheter drainage tubing for kinks or blood clot obstruction and manually irrigate per protocol if occluded
Administer a belladonna and opium suppository immediately without checking catheter patency
Increase the continuous bladder irrigation inflow rate while outflow remains sluggish
Deflate the 30-mL catheter retention balloon to relieve pressure on the bladder neck

rationales.summary: Sudden bladder spasms with dark red sluggish drainage post-TURP usually indicate catheter occlusion by blood clots; patency must be verified before giving antispasmodics or increasing inflow.
rationales.A: Correct. Assessing for kinks and clearing clot obstruction prevents bladder overdistension and venous hemorrhage.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Giving antispasmodics without relieving mechanical obstruction masks bladder distension.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Increasing inflow against an obstructed outflow tract risks bladder rupture or TURP syndrome.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The large balloon provides essential hemostatic tamponade against the prostatic fossa.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 56-year-old female admitted with severe intractable vomiting and high-output nasogastric tube suctioning for 3 days.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lethargic, muscle cramping, shallow respirations.
medications: 0.9% Sodium Chloride with 40 mEq KCl/L IV at 125 mL/hr
provider_orders: Replace NG output mL-for-mL with 0.45% NaCl + 20 mEq KCl/L

questions.stem: How should the nurse interpret this client's arterial blood gas results?

options.text: Partially compensated metabolic alkalosis
Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
Fully compensated metabolic acidosis
Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis

rationales.summary: pH > 7.45 (7.51) indicates alkalemia; elevated HCO3 (35 mEq/L) identifies a metabolic origin from gastric acid loss, and elevated PaCO2 (47 mmHg) shows respiratory hypoventilation attempting to compensate.
rationales.A: Correct. pH is alkaline (7.51), HCO3 is elevated (35 mEq/L), and PaCO2 is elevated (47 mmHg) in partial respiratory compensation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Respiratory acidosis presents with pH < 7.35.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Metabolic acidosis presents with low HCO3 (< 22 mEq/L).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis presents with low PaCO2 (< 35 mmHg).

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 50-year-old male with alcohol use disorder admitted for acute pancreatitis and refractory hypokalemia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes (3+), positive Trousseau sign, tremors.

diagnostic_results.Telemetry: Prolonged QT interval with occasional non-sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes)

medications: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV in 100 mL D5W over 1 hour

questions.stem: Why is it essential to correct hypomagnesemia in order to successfully treat this client's concurrent hypokalemia?

options.text: Magnesium deficiency impairs renal potassium conservation, causing ongoing urinary potassium wasting
Magnesium sulfate chemically binds potassium in the bloodstream to prevent excretion
Hypomagnesemia stimulates excessive aldosterone release from the pituitary gland
Intravenous potassium cannot dissolve in saline unless magnesium is co-infused

rationales.summary: Intracellular magnesium inhibits renal outer medullary potassium (ROMK) channels in the collecting duct; low magnesium leads to unchecked renal potassium wasting.
rationales.A: Correct. Until hypomagnesemia is corrected, the kidneys continue wasting administered potassium, rendering hypokalemia refractory.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Magnesium does not chelate potassium in plasma.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal cortex, not the pituitary gland.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Potassium chloride is fully soluble in normal saline.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 58-year-old male with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis admitted with confusion, inverted sleep-wake cycle, and asterixis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Jaundiced sclera, spider angiomas, moderate ascites, flapping tremor when wrists are dorsiflexed.

diagnostic_results.Abdominal Ultrasound: Nodular cirrhotic liver, patent portal vein, moderate ascites

medications: Lactulose 30 mL PO every 2 hours until bowel movement, then titrate
provider_orders: Titrate lactulose to achieve 2 to 3 soft stools per day

questions.stem: Which assessment finding demonstrates that lactulose therapy is achieving its intended therapeutic outcome?

options.text: Resolution of asterixis, improved orientation, and 2 to 3 soft stools daily
Ten watery stools per day with rising serum sodium
Decrease in abdominal girth by 6 cm within 12 hours
Normalization of serum INR from 1.9 to 1.0

rationales.summary: Lactulose acidifies colonic contents, converting absorbable ammonia (NH3) into non-absorbable ammonium (NH4+) excreted in stool, improving neurological status.
rationales.A: Correct. Cleared sensorium, resolution of asterixis, and 2-3 soft bowel movements per day confirm effective ammonia trapping and excretion.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Excessive watery diarrhea causes dehydration and hypernatremia, which can worsen hepatic encephalopathy.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Lactulose treats encephalopathy, not ascites.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Lactulose does not restore hepatic clotting factor synthesis.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 46-year-old male admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and persistent nausea/vomiting.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Guarding in epigastrium, hypoactive bowel sounds, bluish discoloration around umbilicus (Cullen sign).

diagnostic_results.Abdominal CT: Edematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid collections

medications: Lactated Ringer IV infusion at 200 mL/hr
Hydromorphone 1 mg IV every 3 hours PRN severe pain

questions.stem: Which nursing interventions are appropriate in the acute management of this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administer aggressive intravenous lactated Ringer fluid resuscitation and monitor urine output
Place the client in a side-lying position with knees flexed toward the chest to relieve pain
Maintain NPO status during the acute phase to suppress pancreatic enzyme stimulation
Monitor for hypocalcemia (Chvostek/Trousseau signs) and hyperglycemia
Provide a high-fat diet as soon as nausea subsides to prevent weight loss

rationales.summary: Acute pancreatitis causes third-space hypovolemia, severe retroperitoneal pain, fat saponification (hypocalcemia), and islet dysfunction (hyperglycemia).
rationales.A: Correct. Early goal-directed IV hydration with lactated Ringer prevents pancreatic necrosis and acute kidney injury.
rationales.B: Correct. Flexing the trunk/knees relieves tension on the inflamed retroperitoneal peritoneum.
rationales.C: Correct. Resting the GI tract reduces secretin and cholecystokinin stimulation of pancreatic exocrine secretion.
rationales.D: Correct. Fat necrosis binds calcium (hypocalcemia) and beta-cell inflammation elevates blood glucose.
rationales.E: Incorrect. When feeding resumes, a low-fat diet is introduced gradually.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 64-year-old male admitted to the ICU step-down unit with massive hematemesis from bleeding esophageal varices.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Pale, diaphoretic, drowsy, coughing up bright red blood.

diagnostic_results.History: Portal hypertension secondary to hepatitis C cirrhosis

medications: Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus followed by 50 mcg/hr infusion
provider_orders: Prepare for emergent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with variceal band ligation

questions.stem: Which intervention takes highest priority before transporting this client for emergent endoscopy?

options.text: Prepare for elective endotracheal intubation to protect the airway from massive blood aspiration
Insert a nasogastric tube for iced saline gastric lavage
Administer oral propranolol 40 mg to reduce portal venous pressure
Place the client flat in the supine position for comfort

rationales.summary: Active hematemesis combined with altered mental status (drowsiness) creates extreme aspiration risk during endoscopy; airway protection via intubation is the top priority.
rationales.A: Correct. Airway always comes first; elective intubation prevents fatal aspiration of blood during active variceal hemorrhage and EGD.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Iced saline lavage is outdated and risks mucosal injury and hypothermia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol) are used for primary/secondary prophylaxis, never during acute hemorrhagic hypotension.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Supine positioning promotes aspiration of blood.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 54-year-old female 2 days post-sigmoid colostomy creation for diverticular perforation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Stoma in left lower quadrant is moist, beefy red, and slightly edematous; small amount of serosanguinous fluid in pouch.
medications: Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN
provider_orders: Ostomy nurse consult and client teaching

questions.stem: Which stoma assessment finding would require immediate notification of the surgeon?

options.text: The stoma appears dusky, purplish-black, and dry
The stoma is moist, pink-red, and slightly swollen
Small droplets of blood appear when the stoma mucosa is gently cleansed
Liquid stool drains into the pouch on postoperative day 3

rationales.summary: A healthy stoma is moist and beefy red/pink; a dusky, bluish, or black stoma indicates compromised arterial blood supply and bowel ischemia/necrosis.
rationales.A: Correct. Dusky or black discoloration indicates stomal ischemia or necrosis requiring urgent surgical evaluation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Moist pink-red appearance with mild early postoperative edema is normal.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Minor mucosal oozing during wiping is expected due to rich capillary vascularity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Return of bowel function with liquid-to-pasty output is expected.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 61-year-old male receiving a unit of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) for symptomatic anemia (Hgb 6.8 g/dL).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fifteen minutes after starting the transfusion, the client reports chills, lower back pain, and chest tightness.

questions.stem: Place the nurse's actions in the exact priority sequence from first to last.

items: Disconnect the blood tubing at the hub and infuse 0.9% sodium chloride through new IV tubing
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and vital signs while notifying the provider and blood bank
Return the blood bag and tubing to the blood bank and collect post-transfusion blood and urine samples

correct_response: Disconnect the blood tubing at the hub and infuse 0.9% sodium chloride through new IV tubing
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and vital signs while notifying the provider and blood bank
Return the blood bag and tubing to the blood bank and collect post-transfusion blood and urine samples

rationales.summary: In any suspected transfusion reaction, stopping further infusion of incompatible blood immediately prevents worsening hemolysis, followed by maintaining IV access with new saline tubing.
rationales.1: Stopping the infusion immediately prevents additional incompatible red cells from entering the circulation.
rationales.2: Using new tubing prevents flushing the blood remaining in the old IV tubing into the client while maintaining IV patency for shock resuscitation.
rationales.3: Evaluating vital signs and alerting the provider and blood bank initiates emergency medical treatment and crossmatch investigation.
rationales.4: Returning the blood unit and sending blood/urine specimens confirms hemolysis (free hemoglobin, Coombs test) and prevents renal tubular damage.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 48-year-old female receiving consolidation chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fatigued, oral mucosa pink without lesions, central venous catheter dressing dry and intact.
provider_orders: Notify provider immediately for temperature >= 38.0 C (100.4 F)

questions.stem: Which protective interventions should the nurse implement for this severely neutropenic client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in a private room and enforce strict hand hygiene for all staff and visitors
Remove fresh flowers, potted plants, and standing water pitchers from the room
Avoid rectal temperatures, suppositories, and enemas
Encourage fresh unwashed berries and raw vegetable salads to boost antioxidant intake
Report a single oral temperature of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher immediately as an oncologic emergency

rationales.summary: Severe neutropenia (ANC < 500/mm3) eliminates normal inflammatory signs; infection prevention and immediate recognition of febrile neutropenia are life-saving.
rationales.A: Correct. Private room assignment and hand hygiene reduce exogenous pathogen exposure.
rationales.B: Correct. Soil and stagnant water harbor Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, and other opportunistic pathogens.
rationales.C: Correct. Rectal trauma can cause mucosal tears and gram-negative bacteremia (and bleeding given thrombocytopenia).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Raw unwashed produce can harbor surface bacteria and fungi; thoroughly washed or cooked foods are required.
rationales.E: Correct. Febrile neutropenia requires blood cultures and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 60 minutes.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 52-year-old male with high-grade Burkitt lymphoma 24 hours after starting induction chemotherapy.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports muscle cramps, flank discomfort, and decreased urine output.

questions.stem: Which classic tetrad of laboratory abnormalities characterizes tumor lysis syndrome (TLS)?

options.text: Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia
Hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypouricemia, and hypercalcemia
Hypernatremia, hypercalcemia, hypoglycemia, and metabolic alkalosis
Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypouricemia, and hypermagnesemia

rationales.summary: Rapid tumor cell lysis releases intracellular potassium, phosphorus, and nucleic acids (metabolized to uric acid), while excess phosphorus binds serum calcium causing secondary hypocalcemia.
rationales.A: Correct. Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and secondary hypocalcemia define tumor lysis syndrome.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The potassium, phosphorus, uric acid, and calcium directions are reversed.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hypercalcemia is seen in malignancy-associated bone resorption, not TLS.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Uric acid and phosphorus are elevated, not decreased.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 25-year-old male with sickle cell anemia admitted with severe bilateral femur and lower back pain (9/10) following a cold-weather trip.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Grimacing in pain, scleral icterus, extremities cool to touch.
provider_orders: Incentive spirometry every hour while awake

questions.stem: Which combination of initial nursing priorities best addresses the pathophysiology of an acute vaso-occlusive sickle cell crisis?

options.text: Aggressive hydration, scheduled/PCA opioid analgesia, and oxygen if hypoxemic
Fluid restriction, cold compresses to painful joints, and aspirin
Diuretic therapy, high-intensity ambulation, and acetaminophen alone
Iron supplementation, bed rest with legs dependent, and meperidine

rationales.summary: Hydration reduces blood viscosity and sickling, potent opioid analgesia treats severe ischemic pain, and oxygen corrects hypoxemia.
rationales.A: Correct. Hydration, effective opioid analgesia, warmth, and incentive spirometry (to prevent acute chest syndrome) are the pillars of vaso-occlusive crisis care.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Dehydration and cold packs promote vasoconstriction and further RBC sickling.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Diuretics worsen viscosity, and acetaminophen alone is inadequate for severe ischemic crisis pain.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Meperidine is contraindicated due to its neurotoxic metabolite normeperidine causing seizures, and iron overload is common in sickle cell patients.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 32-year-old male 8 hours post-open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a comminuted right tibial shaft fracture with a circumferential plaster cast.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports severe, escalating right lower leg pain (10/10) unrelieved by IV hydromorphone given 30 minutes ago; excruciating pain when the nurse passively dorsiflexes his right great toe; toes are tense and pale.
medications: Hydromorphone 1 mg IV every 3 hours PRN pain

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take immediately?

options.text: Notify the orthopedic surgeon immediately to bivalve/split the cast and place the leg at heart level
Elevate the casted leg higher on three pillows and apply ice packs directly over the cast
Reassure the client that severe throbbing pain is expected for 48 hours after tibial surgery
Wait until the dorsalis pedis pulse disappears before contacting the surgeon

rationales.summary: Pain out of proportion to injury unrelieved by opioids and pain with passive stretch are the earliest hallmark signs of acute compartment syndrome requiring immediate cast release.
rationales.A: Correct. Splitting/bivalving the cast relieves external pressure, and positioning at heart level (not elevated) preserves arterial inflow while awaiting potential fasciotomy.
rationales.B: Incorrect. High elevation reduces arterial perfusion pressure into the tense compartment, and ice induces vasoconstriction.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Pain refractory to opioids with passive stretch pain is an orthopedic emergency, not routine post-op pain.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Pulselessness is a late sign indicating irreversible muscle and nerve necrosis (within 4-6 hours).

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 40-year-old male weighing 80 kg brought to the burn center immediately after sustaining deep partial- and full-thickness thermal burns over 40% of his total body surface area (TBSA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, hoarse voice, singed nasal hairs, circumferential burns on anterior trunk and bilateral upper extremities.
provider_orders: Parkland formula fluid resuscitation: 4 mL x weight (kg) x %TBSA over 24 hours (half in first 8 hours)

questions.stem: Using the Parkland formula (4 mL x 80 kg x 40% TBSA), calculate the hourly infusion rate in mL/hr for the first 8 hours following the burn injury. Enter a whole number only.

rationales.summary: Total 24-hour Parkland volume = 4 mL x 80 kg x 40 = 12,800 mL. Half (6,400 mL) is infused over the first 8 hours: 6,400 mL / 8 hr = 800 mL/hr.
rationales.calculation: 4 mL x 80 kg x 40 = 12,800 mL total in 24 hours. First 8 hours = 12,800 / 2 = 6,400 mL. Hourly rate = 6,400 mL / 8 hr = 800 mL/hr.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 68-year-old female admitted with septic shock requiring continuous norepinephrine vasopressor support.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Warm flushed skin, capillary refill 3 seconds, central venous catheter in right internal jugular vein.
provider_orders: Start norepinephrine at 8 mcg/min and titrate to maintain MAP >= 65 mmHg

questions.stem: The pharmacy supplies norepinephrine 4 mg in 250 mL D5W. At what rate in mL/hr should the nurse program the infusion pump to deliver 8 mcg/min? Enter a whole number only.

rationales.summary: Concentration = 4,000 mcg / 250 mL = 16 mcg/mL. Desired dose = 8 mcg/min x 60 min/hr = 480 mcg/hr. Rate = 480 mcg/hr / 16 mcg/mL = 30 mL/hr.
rationales.calculation: 4 mg = 4,000 mcg. 4,000 mcg / 250 mL = 16 mcg/mL. 8 mcg/min x 60 min = 480 mcg/hr. 480 / 16 = 30 mL/hr.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 53-year-old male receiving intravenous vancomycin 1.5 g in 250 mL normal saline for MRSA bacteremia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fifteen minutes into the infusion, the client develops bright red erythematous flushing over his face, neck, and upper chest with pruritus.
provider_orders: Infuse vancomycin over at least 90-120 minutes

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Stop the vancomycin infusion, assess vital signs and airway, and notify the provider for an antihistamine and slower infusion rate
Increase the infusion rate so the remaining dose finishes within 15 minutes
Document a life-threatening IgE-mediated anaphylactic allergy and permanently discard the vancomycin
Apply hydrocortisone cream to the neck and continue the current infusion rate

rationales.summary: Vancomycin infusion reaction ('red man syndrome') is a rate-dependent non-IgE histamine release from mast cells caused by infusing vancomycin too rapidly.
rationales.A: Correct. Pausing the infusion, assessing hemodynamics/airway (to rule out true anaphylaxis), administering diphenhydramine, and resuming at a slower rate (over >=90-120 min) resolves the reaction.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Faster infusion worsens histamine release and can trigger severe hypotension.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rate-related histamine flushing is not a true IgE-mediated allergy and does not preclude future slow administration.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Continuing a rapid infusion exacerbates systemic histamine release.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 69-year-old female receiving intravenous gentamicin for complicated pyelonephritis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports new ringing in both ears and mild dizziness when sitting on the edge of the bed.
provider_orders: Draw peak and trough levels around third dose

questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate based on these findings? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hold the next scheduled dose of gentamicin and notify the provider immediately
Document tinnitus and vertigo as signs of cranial nerve VIII ototoxicity
Monitor hourly urine output and daily serum creatinine for nephrotoxicity
Administer the scheduled dose and draw a peak level 30 minutes later
Implement fall precautions due to vestibular dysfunction

rationales.summary: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin) cause dose-limiting nephrotoxicity and irreversible eighth cranial nerve (auditory/vestibular) ototoxicity.
rationales.A: Correct. An elevated trough (>2 mcg/mL), rising creatinine, and tinnitus require holding the dose and alerting the provider.
rationales.B: Correct. Tinnitus and disequilibrium reflect cochlear and vestibular damage to CN VIII.
rationales.C: Correct. Proximal renal tubular accumulation causes acute kidney injury.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Giving another dose with a toxic trough risks permanent deafness and renal failure.
rationales.E: Correct. Vestibular toxicity impairs balance and increases fall risk.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 45-year-old female 2 hours post-abdominal hysterectomy receiving morphine via patient-controlled analgesia (PCA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Unarousable to sternal rub, pinpoint pupils (1 mm), snoring respirations.
medications: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV PRN respiratory depression

questions.stem: After stopping the morphine PCA, supporting ventilation, and administering naloxone IV, what ongoing assessment is critical because of naloxone's pharmacokinetics?

options.text: Monitor respiratory rate and sedation closely for at least 1 to 2 hours because naloxone has a shorter half-life than morphine
Leave the client unmonitored once she awakens because one dose of naloxone permanently clears morphine
Immediately restart the morphine PCA at the previous basal rate once respiratory rate reaches 12 breaths/min
Administer flumazenil 0.2 mg IV as a synergistic opioid antagonist

rationales.summary: Naloxone has a short elimination half-life (30-60 minutes) compared to morphine (2-4 hours), so respiratory depression can recur once naloxone wears off.
rationales.A: Correct. Renarcotization commonly occurs 30-60 minutes after naloxone administration, necessitating continuous monitoring and possible repeat dosing.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Naloxone competitively antagonizes mu-opioid receptors temporarily; it does not accelerate morphine metabolism.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Restarting the PCA immediately would re-induce respiratory arrest.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 58-year-old female admitted with severe dehydration and hypokalemia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, weak peripheral pulses, dry oral mucosa, peripheral IV catheter in left forearm.

diagnostic_results.ECG: Flattened T waves with prominent U waves

medications: Potassium chloride 40 mEq in 1,000 mL 0.9% Sodium Chloride IV at 125 mL/hr
provider_orders: Verify urine output >= 30 mL/hr prior to potassium infusion

questions.stem: Which safety rule must the nurse follow strictly when administering intravenous potassium chloride?

options.text: Never administer potassium chloride by direct IV push and always infuse diluted via an infusion pump
Administer concentrated potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push over 2 minutes for severe hypokalemia
Infuse potassium chloride at 40 mEq/hr through a hand vein without cardiac monitoring
Administer potassium even if the client has been anuric for 8 hours

rationales.summary: Undiluted or rapid IV push potassium chloride causes immediate fatal cardiac arrest in diastole; it must always be diluted and controlled by an infusion pump.
rationales.A: Correct. Potassium chloride is a high-alert medication requiring dilution, infusion pump control (typically <=10 mEq/hr peripherally), and verification of adequate urine output.
rationales.B: Incorrect. IV push KCl is lethal.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rates >10-20 mEq/hr require central venous access and continuous ECG monitoring.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Oliguria/anuria prevents renal potassium excretion and causes lethal hyperkalemia.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 56-year-old male started on lisinopril 10 mg daily 3 weeks ago for stage 2 hypertension.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports a persistent, dry, nonproductive hacking cough that started 1 week ago; lungs clear, no fever or dyspnea.

questions.stem: What is the most likely cause of this client's dry cough, and what action should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Bradykinin accumulation caused by lisinopril; anticipate switching to an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) such as losartan
Early pulmonary edema; anticipate adding oral furosemide
Hospital-acquired bacterial bronchitis; anticipate starting azithromycin
Normal transient side effect; instruct the client to take dextromethorphan daily

rationales.summary: ACE inhibitors prevent the breakdown of bradykinin and substance P in the respiratory tract, causing a characteristic dry cough in 5%-20% of clients.
rationales.A: Correct. Bradykinin-mediated cough resolves only after discontinuing the ACE inhibitor and switching to an ARB (which does not inhibit bradykinin degradation).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lungs are clear and vital signs are normal.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Absence of fever, sputum, or lung sounds rules against bacterial infection.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Antitussives do not relieve ACE-inhibitor cough.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 37-year-old male taking oral phenytoin 100 mg three times daily for focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild gingival hyperplasia, gait steady, alert and oriented.
medications: Phenytoin 100 mg PO three times daily
provider_orders: Continue current dose and reinforce medication teaching

questions.stem: Which instructions should the nurse include when educating this client about long-term phenytoin therapy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Perform meticulous oral hygiene with a soft toothbrush, floss daily, and schedule regular dental cleanings
Report any new skin rash, fever, or mouth ulcers immediately to the healthcare provider
Never stop taking phenytoin abruptly, as doing so can trigger status epilepticus
Switch freely between different generic brands of phenytoin to save money
Report ataxia, slurred speech, or nystagmus as signs of drug toxicity

rationales.summary: Phenytoin teaching covers gingival hyperplasia prevention, serious cutaneous reactions (SJS/TEN), narrow therapeutic index consistency, and neurotoxic symptoms.
rationales.A: Correct. Good oral hygiene and gum massage minimize phenytoin-induced gingival overgrowth.
rationales.B: Correct. Morbilliform or blistering rash can herald Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.
rationales.C: Correct. Abrupt withdrawal precipitates rebound seizures and status epilepticus.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Phenytoin has nonlinear zero-order pharmacokinetics; switching brands can cause subtherapeutic or toxic levels.
rationales.E: Correct. Nystagmus, ataxia, and dysarthria indicate serum levels > 20 mcg/mL.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 41-year-old female taking lithium carbonate for bipolar I disorder who developed viral gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Coarse hand tremors, slurred speech, ataxia, drowsiness.
medications: Lithium carbonate 300 mg PO three times daily

questions.stem: Which physiological relationship explains why dehydration and thiazide diuretics precipitated lithium toxicity in this client?

options.text: The kidneys reabsorb lithium in place of sodium in the proximal tubule whenever sodium or volume is depleted
Thiazide diuretics block hepatic cytochrome P450 metabolism of lithium
Dehydration accelerates intestinal absorption of sustained-release lithium
Low serum sodium displaces lithium from plasma albumin binding sites

rationales.summary: Lithium is a monovalent cation handled similarly to sodium by the proximal renal tubule; volume/sodium depletion triggers avid proximal reabsorption of both sodium and lithium.
rationales.A: Correct. Sodium depletion from GI losses or thiazides increases proximal tubular lithium reabsorption, causing toxic serum accumulation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lithium is not metabolized by the liver; it is excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Toxicity is driven by reduced renal clearance rather than faster GI absorption.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Lithium is not bound to plasma proteins.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 51-year-old female receiving continuous total parenteral nutrition (TPN) via a right subclavian central venous catheter for severe Crohn enterocutaneous fistula.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, central line dressing clean and dry; nurse notices the current TPN bag has 15 mL remaining and the new bag from pharmacy is delayed by 45 minutes.
medications: TPN (20% dextrose, amino acids, electrolytes) infusing at 85 mL/hr
provider_orders: Change TPN bag and tubing every 24 hours

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take when the current TPN bag runs out before the replacement bag arrives?

options.text: Infuse 10% dextrose in water (D10W) at 85 mL/hr until the new TPN bag arrives
Flush the catheter with 0.9% sodium chloride and cap it until the pharmacy delivers the TPN
Infuse lactated Ringer solution at 85 mL/hr
Slow the remaining 15 mL of TPN to 10 mL/hr so it lasts for 90 minutes

rationales.summary: High endogenous insulin levels stimulated by concentrated dextrose in TPN persist after abrupt discontinuation, causing severe rebound hypoglycemia unless D10W is infused.
rationales.A: Correct. Infusing D10W at the same hourly rate prevents rebound hypoglycemia until the new TPN bag is hung.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Capping the line without dextrose causes rapid rebound hypoglycemia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Lactated Ringer contains no dextrose and will not prevent hypoglycemia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Altering TPN infusion rates unpredictably disrupts glucose homeostasis.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 59-year-old male prescribed allopurinol 100 mg PO daily for chronic tophaceous gout.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild non-tender tophi on right olecranon; currently free of acute joint inflammation.

questions.stem: Which instruction is most important for the nurse to emphasize when teaching this client about allopurinol?

options.text: Stop taking allopurinol and notify the provider immediately if any skin rash develops
Take allopurinol only when experiencing sudden severe big-toe pain
Restrict fluid intake to prevent swelling in the lower extremities
Take aspirin 650 mg daily alongside allopurinol to speed uric acid excretion

rationales.summary: Allopurinol can trigger severe cutaneous adverse reactions (allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome / Stevens-Johnson syndrome), so any rash requires immediate discontinuation.
rationales.A: Correct. Even a mild maculopapular rash can progress to fatal Stevens-Johnson syndrome/DRESS; allopurinol must be stopped immediately.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Allopurinol is a daily urate-lowering maintenance drug, not an acute anti-inflammatory analgesic.
rationales.C: Incorrect. High fluid intake (2-3 L/day) prevents uric acid renal calculi.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Low-to-moderate dose aspirin inhibits renal uric acid excretion and precipitates gout flares.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 32-year-old G1P0 at 35 weeks gestation receiving intravenous magnesium sulfate at 2 g/hr for severe preeclampsia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Somnolent, absent patellar deep tendon reflexes, skin flushed.
medications: Magnesium sulfate 40 g in 1,000 mL LR at 50 mL/hr (2 g/hr)
provider_orders: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV at bedside

questions.stem: Which sequence of actions should the nurse perform immediately?

options.text: Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion, apply oxygen, prepare to administer calcium gluconate 1 g IV, and notify the provider
Decrease the magnesium infusion rate to 1 g/hr and recheck reflexes in 1 hour
Administer a 500 mL bolus of magnesium sulfate to improve placental perfusion
Administer naloxone 0.4 mg IV push to reverse respiratory depression

rationales.summary: Loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate < 12 breaths/min, and oliguria indicate magnesium toxicity requiring immediate infusion cessation and IV calcium gluconate.
rationales.A: Correct. Stopping the infusion halts further neuromuscular blockade, while calcium gluconate directly antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Continuing magnesium in the presence of areflexia and bradypnea risks respiratory and cardiac arrest.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Giving more magnesium would be lethal.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 34-year-old male taking clozapine 300 mg PO daily for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Presents to the outpatient clinic reporting a sore throat, malaise, and chills for 24 hours.

questions.stem: Which action is the nurse's top priority?

options.text: Hold the clozapine dose and obtain a STAT complete blood count (CBC) with absolute neutrophil count (ANC)
Reassure the client that sore throat is a normal anticholinergic side effect and continue clozapine
Advise the client to take ibuprofen and return next week for his routine monthly blood draw
Double the evening clozapine dose to prevent psychotic relapse during illness

rationales.summary: Clozapine carries a black-box warning for severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis; fever and sore throat must be evaluated immediately with a STAT ANC before giving another dose.
rationales.A: Correct. Flu-like symptoms, fever, or sore throat can be the earliest clinical signs of life-threatening agranulocytosis.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Clozapine causes sialorrhea (hypersalivation) rather than dry throat, and fever/sore throat cannot be dismissed.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Delaying ANC evaluation risks overwhelming sepsis.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Increasing clozapine without verifying ANC is unsafe.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 28-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks gestation in active labor at 6 cm dilation, membranes artificially ruptured 20 minutes ago.
clinical_scenario.assessment: External fetal monitor shows a baseline FHR of 140 bpm with moderate variability, punctuated by abrupt V-shaped drops in FHR to 95 bpm lasting 25 seconds with rapid return to baseline.

questions.stem: What is the primary cause of these fetal heart rate decelerations, and which nursing action should be performed first?

options.text: Umbilical cord compression; reposition the client laterally or into knee-chest position
Fetal head compression; document as a benign finding and continue current care
Uteroplacental insufficiency; prepare immediately for an emergent cesarean birth
Maternal supine hypotension; administer an IV bolus of ephedrine

rationales.summary: Abrupt V- or W-shaped drops in FHR (variable decelerations) reflect transient umbilical cord compression, especially after rupture of membranes.
rationales.A: Correct. Variable decelerations indicate cord compression; changing maternal position (left/right lateral or knee-chest) relieves mechanical pressure on the umbilical cord.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Head compression causes uniform early decelerations that mirror contractions.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Uteroplacental insufficiency causes gradual late decelerations peaking after the contraction peak.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Maternal BP is normal (118/72 mmHg).

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 30-year-old G4P4 45 minutes after vaginal delivery of a 4,350 g infant following prolonged oxytocin induction.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Perineal pad saturated with bright red blood and large clots within 15 minutes; uterine fundus palpated 3 cm above the umbilicus, boggy, and deviated to the right.
medications: Oxytocin 20 units in 1,000 mL LR infusing at 125 mL/hr

questions.stem: Which sequence of immediate nursing interventions is most appropriate?

options.text: Perform firm bimanual/fundal massage while supporting the lower uterine segment, call for assistance, and empty the urinary bladder
Administer methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM first without touching the uterus
Insert vaginal gauze packing and elevate the head of the bed to 45 degrees
Encourage the client to ambulate to the bathroom to void

rationales.summary: Uterine atony is the leading cause of postpartum hemorrhage; immediate firm fundal massage (anchoring the lower uterine segment) stimulates myometrial contraction, while bladder emptying corrects fundal displacement.
rationales.A: Correct. Firm fundal massage with lower-segment support immediately compresses bleeding spiral arteries, while catheterizing a full bladder removes mechanical displacement of the uterus.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Mechanical fundal massage is always the immediate first-line action while uterotonics are prepared.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Loose vaginal packing conceals ongoing blood loss and does not contract an atonic myometrium.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A hypotensive, tachycardic bleeding client must remain supine/flat with straight catheterization performed at the bedside.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 34-year-old G1P0 at 34 weeks gestation admitted with severe preeclampsia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Reports right upper quadrant epigastric pain, nausea, and visual scotomata; 2+ pitting pedal edema.
medications: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose then 2 g/hr
provider_orders: Prepare for delivery after maternal stabilization

questions.stem: Which nursing interventions are essential for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid abdominal palpation over the liver to prevent subcapsular hepatic hematoma rupture
Maintain a quiet, dimly lit environment with padded side rails for seizure prophylaxis
Monitor blood pressure every 5 to 15 minutes during IV labetalol administration
Administer intramuscular betamethasone into the gluteal muscle without applying prolonged pressure
Type and crossmatch for platelets and packed red blood cells prior to delivery

rationales.summary: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) carries high risk of hepatic capsule rupture, eclamptic seizures, stroke, and hemorrhage.
rationales.A: Correct. Hepatic congestion and subcapsular hematoma make liver palpation hazardous.
rationales.B: Correct. Minimizing sensory stimulation alongside magnesium sulfate reduces eclamptic seizure risk.
rationales.C: Correct. Frequent BP checks ensure severe hypertension (<160/110 mmHg) is safely controlled without causing placental hypoperfusion.
rationales.D: Incorrect. With platelets at 68,000/mm3, firm prolonged pressure is required after any IM injection to prevent hematoma.
rationales.E: Correct. Thrombocytopenia necessitates blood product readiness for delivery.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 31-year-old G3P2 at 33 weeks gestation brought to labor and delivery triage with sudden onset of painless, bright red vaginal bleeding.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Uterus is soft, relaxed, and nontender; fetal head is high and floating.

questions.stem: Which procedure is strictly contraindicated in this client until placental location is confirmed by ultrasound?

options.text: Digital vaginal cervical examination
Transabdominal obstetric ultrasound
External electronic fetal heart rate monitoring
Insertion of a large-bore peripheral intravenous catheter

rationales.summary: Painless bright red bleeding in the third trimester with a soft nontender uterus is classic for placenta previa; digital vaginal exams can lacerate the low-lying placenta and cause catastrophic hemorrhage.
rationales.A: Correct. Digital vaginal examination is strictly contraindicated until placenta previa is ruled out by ultrasound.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Transabdominal ultrasound is the safe diagnostic gold standard.
rationales.C: Incorrect. External fetal monitoring is essential and noninvasive.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Large-bore IV access is a critical safety measure.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 2-hour-old term male infant born to a mother with gestational diabetes mellitus; birth weight 4,280 g (LGA).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Jittery extremities, weak high-pitched cry, mild hypotonia.

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take first for this jittery newborn with a blood glucose of 32 mg/dL?

options.text: Initiate an immediate oral feeding (breastfeed or infant formula) and recheck heel-stick glucose in 30 minutes
Administer 5% dextrose in water (D5W) orally via syringe
Observe the newborn for 1 hour and recheck glucose if jitteriness worsens
Place the newborn under a radiant warmer without feeding to conserve calories

rationales.summary: Infants of diabetic mothers have transient hyperinsulinemia after umbilical cord clamping; asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic newborns able to feed orally require immediate breastmilk or formula.
rationales.A: Correct. Breastmilk or formula provides sustained complex carbohydrates, protein, and fat to stabilize blood glucose without triggering rebound insulin spikes.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Oral dextrose water causes a rapid glucose spike followed by rebound insulin secretion and worse hypoglycemia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Delaying treatment risks hypoglycemic seizures and neuronal injury.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Maintaining normothermia is important, but caloric substrate via feeding is immediately required.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 38-hour-old term female newborn receiving overhead LED phototherapy for unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Jaundiced skin over face and upper chest, vigorous suck, 4 wet diapers and 2 transitional stools in past 24 hours.

questions.stem: Which nursing interventions are essential while this newborn is receiving phototherapy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply opaque eye shields over closed eyelids and remove them during feedings to inspect the eyes
Keep the newborn undressed except for a small diaper and eye shields to maximize skin exposure
Apply moisturizing lotion to the newborn's skin every 4 hours to prevent dryness
Monitor axillary temperature every 2 to 4 hours and encourage frequent breastfeedings
Turn the phototherapy light off when drawing blood samples for serum bilirubin levels

rationales.summary: Phototherapy photo-isomerizes unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble lumirubin excreted in bile and urine; care focuses on retinal protection, skin exposure, hydration, and accurate bilirubin sampling.
rationales.A: Correct. Opaque shields protect the developing retina from light damage, and periodic removal allows parent-infant bonding and conjunctival checks.
rationales.B: Correct. Maximum exposed skin surface accelerates bilirubin photo-isomerization.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Lotions or ointments absorb heat under phototherapy lights and can cause thermal burns.
rationales.D: Correct. Frequent feeding promotes stooling (bilirubin excretion) and offsets insensible water loss.
rationales.E: Correct. Phototherapy light degrades bilirubin inside the capillary blood collection tube, causing falsely low lab results.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 26-year-old G1P1 postpartum client 12 hours after an uncomplicated vaginal birth.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fundus firm at umbilicus, lochia rubra moderate, perineum intact.
medications: Rho(D) immune globulin 300 mcg IM ordered
provider_orders: Administer Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours of delivery

questions.stem: Which explanation accurately describes why this client needs Rho(D) immune globulin?

options.text: To prevent her immune system from forming anti-Rh antibodies that could attack red blood cells in a future Rh-positive fetus
To treat active hemolytic anemia in her current newborn infant
To provide passive immunity against maternal rubella infection
To stimulate maternal bone marrow production of Rh-positive red blood cells

rationales.summary: When an unsensitized Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive infant, Rho(D) immune globulin clears fetal Rh-positive RBCs from maternal circulation before maternal sensitization occurs.
rationales.A: Correct. Administering Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours prevents isoimmunization and hemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn in subsequent pregnancies.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The newborn's direct Coombs is negative; Rho(D) immune globulin is given to the mother, not the infant.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rubella vaccine provides active rubella immunity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Blood type is genetically determined and cannot be altered.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 29-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks gestation in labor; spontaneous rupture of membranes occurs during a contraction.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Fetal heart rate abruptly drops from 140 bpm to 65 bpm with prolonged bradycardia; on sterile vaginal inspection, a pulsating loop of umbilical cord is palpated in the vagina.

questions.stem: Which action must the nurse perform immediately and maintain until emergency cesarean delivery?

options.text: Insert two sterile-gloved fingers into the vagina to lift the fetal presenting part off the umbilical cord while calling for emergency help
Gently push the prolapsed umbilical cord back inside the uterine cavity
Place the client in high Fowler position and encourage forceful pushing
Apply dry sterile gauze over the prolapsed cord and await spontaneous vaginal delivery

rationales.summary: Overt umbilical cord prolapse compresses fetal blood supply; continuous manual elevation of the presenting part (paired with Trendelenburg/knee-chest positioning and stopping oxytocin) preserves fetal oxygenation until cesarean delivery.
rationales.A: Correct. Keeping the examiner's hand in place to elevate the presenting part off the cord prevents cord occlusion until the infant is delivered.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Attempting to push the cord back into the uterus causes severe vasospasm and trauma.
rationales.C: Incorrect. High Fowler and pushing drive the fetal head downward, crushing the cord.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Dry gauze adheres to and desiccates Wharton jelly; warm saline-soaked gauze is used only if cord protrudes externally, and immediate cesarean is mandatory.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 4-year-old unvaccinated boy brought to the emergency department with sudden high fever, severe sore throat, and muffled voice.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sitting upright leaning forward with chin thrust out (tripod position), drooling saliva, inspiratory stridor, anxious expression.

laboratory_results.Pending: Defer blood draws until airway secured

diagnostic_results.Pending: Portable lateral neck X-ray at bedside if stable

medications: Ceftriaxone IV ordered once airway secured
provider_orders: Pediatric anesthesia and ENT STAT to bedside

questions.stem: Which action is strictly contraindicated in the immediate management of this child?

options.text: Inspecting the posterior pharynx with a tongue depressor or obtaining a throat swab
Allowing the child to remain upright in his parent's lap with blow-by humidified oxygen
Notifying pediatric anesthesia and otolaryngology immediately for controlled intubation
Maintaining a calm, quiet environment to prevent crying and agitation

rationales.summary: Tripod positioning, drooling, dysphagia, and high fever indicate acute epiglottitis; any pharyngeal stimulation or agitation can trigger lethal laryngospasm and complete airway occlusion.
rationales.A: Correct. Using a tongue blade or throat swab can provoke immediate reflex laryngospasm and respiratory arrest.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Keeping the child upright with parent comfort and blow-by oxygen minimizes crying and airway collapse.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Controlled intubation in the operating room by specialists is the standard definitive airway management.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Preventing agitation reduces oxygen demand and airway turbulence.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 3-year-old female admitted with 6 days of persistent high fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, cracked red lips, and polymorphous rash.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Irritable, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of hands and feet.
medications: Aspirin 80 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours initially, then low-dose 3-5 mg/kg/day
provider_orders: Serial echocardiograms at baseline, 2 weeks, and 6-8 weeks

questions.stem: Which nursing interventions and parent teachings are appropriate for this child? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor cardiac status closely for arrhythmias, gallop rhythm, or signs of heart failure during IVIG infusion
Delay live-virus immunizations (MMR and varicella) for 11 months after high-dose IVIG administration
Explain that low-dose aspirin therapy continues at home to prevent coronary artery thrombosis
Apply petroleum jelly to cracked lips and offer cool liquids and soft foods
Administer ibuprofen alongside aspirin to accelerate fever resolution

rationales.summary: Kawasaki disease is an acute systemic vasculitis with a high risk of coronary artery aneurysms; treatment combines IVIG and aspirin alongside live-vaccine deferral.
rationales.A: Correct. Myocarditis and volume overload during high-dose IVIG (2 g/kg) require close cardiac monitoring.
rationales.B: Correct. Passively transferred antibodies in IVIG neutralize live MMR and varicella vaccines for up to 11 months.
rationales.C: Correct. Low-dose aspirin provides antiplatelet prophylaxis against coronary aneurysm thrombosis.
rationales.D: Correct. Comfort measures relieve mucositis and maintain hydration.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Ibuprofen competitively blocks aspirin's antiplatelet COX-1 acetylation and increases GI bleeding risk.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 5-week-old male infant admitted with forceful, non-bilious projectile vomiting immediately after every feeding for 4 days.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Hungry immediately after vomiting, sunken anterior fontanelle, visible left-to-right peristaltic waves across upper abdomen, palpable olive-shaped mass in right upper quadrant.
medications: 0.9% Sodium Chloride IV bolus followed by D5 0.45% NaCl with 20 mEq KCl/L
provider_orders: Correct fluid and electrolyte imbalances prior to laparoscopic pyloromyotomy

questions.stem: Why must fluid and electrolyte abnormalities be corrected before the infant undergoes pyloromyotomy?

options.text: Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia increase the risk of postoperative apnea and cardiac arrhythmias under general anesthesia
Preoperative hydration shrinks the hypertrophied pyloric muscle so surgery may be avoided
Alkalosis prevents surgical wound healing by inhibiting fibroblast proliferation
Intravenous fluids are required to dissolve bilious concretions in the duodenum

rationales.summary: Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid causes hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, which depresses central respiratory drive and predisposes the infant to postoperative apnea.
rationales.A: Correct. Pyloromyotomy is an urgent (not emergent) procedure; normalizing volume, chloride, potassium, and pH prevents anesthesia-related apnea and arrhythmias.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Surgical pyloromyotomy is definitive; fluids do not shrink the hypertrophied muscle.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The primary risk is perioperative respiratory depression and arrhythmia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Vomiting in pyloric stenosis is non-bilious because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 9-month-old male brought to the emergency department for episodic inconsolable crying where he draws his knees up to his abdomen every 15 minutes, followed by lethargy.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Sausage-shaped mass palpated in right upper quadrant; diaper contains dark red mucoid stool ('currant jelly' stool).

diagnostic_results.Abdominal Ultrasound: Classic 'target sign' (telescoping of ileum into cecum)

provider_orders: Prepare for ultrasound-guided hydrostatic/pneumatic enema reduction

questions.stem: Immediately before transporting the infant to radiology for the hydrostatic enema, the nurse observes a normal brown stool in the diaper and the infant is resting comfortably without pain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the radiologist and pediatric surgeon immediately because the intussusception may have spontaneously reduced
Discard the diaper and proceed with the enema as scheduled
Offer the infant 4 ounces of oral formula to confirm bowel patency
Administer an opioid analgesic for presumed sedation

rationales.summary: Passage of normal brown stool accompanied by sudden resolution of paroxysmal pain indicates spontaneous reduction of the telescoped bowel segment.
rationales.A: Correct. The provider must be alerted immediately to re-evaluate the infant before performing an invasive enema.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Proceeding without notifying the team could subject the infant to an unnecessary procedure.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Keep the infant NPO until cleared by the surgical/radiology team.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The infant is comfortable and pain-free.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 6-month-old infant with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot hospitalized for bronchiolitis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: During phlebotomy, the infant begins crying vigorously and develops acute deep circumoral and generalized cyanosis with rapid breathing.

diagnostic_results.Echocardiogram: VSD, overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, RVH

medications: Morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV/subcutaneous PRN hypercyanotic spell

questions.stem: Place the nurse's interventions for this acute hypercyanotic ('Tet') spell in the correct priority order from first to last.

items: Place the infant immediately in the knee-chest position while calming the infant
Administer prescribed morphine sulfate to relax infundibular spasm and reduce agitation
Administer prescribed intravenous normal saline bolus to improve right ventricular filling and pulmonary blood flow

correct_response: Place the infant immediately in the knee-chest position while calming the infant
Administer prescribed morphine sulfate to relax infundibular spasm and reduce agitation
Administer prescribed intravenous normal saline bolus to improve right ventricular filling and pulmonary blood flow

rationales.summary: Knee-chest positioning immediately increases systemic vascular resistance, reversing the right-to-left shunt across the VSD and forcing blood into the pulmonary artery.
rationales.1: Knee-chest positioning kinks femoral arteries, raising systemic vascular resistance within seconds to reduce right-to-left shunting.
rationales.2: 100% oxygen acts as a pulmonary vasodilator and maximizes oxygen delivery.
rationales.3: Morphine reduces respiratory drive hyperpnea and relieves right ventricular infundibular spasm.
rationales.4: Isotonic fluid volume expands preload to overcome right ventricular outflow obstruction.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 3-month-old infant 4 hours post-cheiloplasty (cleft lip repair).
clinical_scenario.assessment: Lip suture line intact with Logan bow/protective dressing, mild serous oozing, infant awake and sucking on fingers.
medications: Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO/PR every 6 hours PRN pain
provider_orders: Clear liquids via specialized syringe/Haberman feeder

questions.stem: Which nursing intervention is essential to protect the surgical suture line after cleft lip repair?

options.text: Position the infant supine or side-lying (never prone) and apply soft elbow restraints
Offer a standard pacifier between feedings to soothe crying
Place the infant in the prone position to facilitate oral secretion drainage
Cleanse the suture line vigorously with dry gauze after every feeding

rationales.summary: Preventing mechanical tension or friction on the repaired lip requires supine/side-lying positioning, elbow restraints, and avoiding pacifiers or straws.
rationales.A: Correct. Supine/side-lying positioning prevents rubbing the face against bedding, and elbow restraints prevent hands from touching the suture line.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Pacifiers place direct tension on the fresh lip incision.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Prone positioning causes friction against the mattress and risks suture dehiscence.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Gentle dabbing with sterile saline/water using a cotton-tipped applicator preserves crust-free healing without trauma.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 7-year-old male admitted 2 weeks after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis with periorbital edema and dark smoky-brown urine.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Periorbital and facial puffiness worse in the morning, mild headache, bibasilar crackles.

questions.stem: Which complication is the highest priority for the nurse to monitor in this child during the acute phase?

options.text: Hypertensive encephalopathy and acute pulmonary edema from sodium and water retention
Hypovolemic shock from massive urinary protein wasting
Severe hypoglycemia from impaired renal gluconeogenesis
Spontaneous bone fractures from hypocalcemia

rationales.summary: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis reduces glomerular filtration rate, causing fluid and sodium retention that can precipitate hypertensive encephalopathy and pulmonary edema.
rationales.A: Correct. Monitoring blood pressure, neuro status (headache, visual changes, seizures), and lung sounds detects hypertensive crisis and fluid overload early.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Massive proteinuria and hypovolemia characterize nephrotic syndrome, whereas PSGN presents with hematuria, fluid overload, and hypertension.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia is not a primary complication of PSGN.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Bone fractures are associated with chronic kidney disease-mineral bone disorder, not acute PSGN.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 18-month-old toddler brought to the clinic with 24 hours of watery diarrhea and 3 episodes of vomiting from viral gastroenteritis.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Alert, slightly dry oral mucosa, tears present when crying, capillary refill 2 seconds, 4% weight loss from baseline.
medications: Ondansetron 2 mg orally disintegrating tablet once
provider_orders: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) 50 mL/kg over 4 hours

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give the parent for administering oral rehydration solution (ORS) to this toddler?

options.text: Offer 5 to 10 mL of commercial oral rehydration solution via syringe or spoon every 5 minutes, gradually increasing as tolerated
Give 8 ounces of undiluted apple juice or sports drink quickly to replace lost fluids
Withhold all solid foods and milk for 72 hours until diarrhea completely stops
Administer over-the-counter loperamide liquid after every loose stool

rationales.summary: Frequent small aliquots (5-10 mL every 5 minutes) of balanced glucose-electrolyte ORS prevent gastric distension and emesis while utilizing sodium-glucose cotransport.
rationales.A: Correct. Small, frequent volumes allow effective intestinal absorption without triggering the vomiting reflex.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Apple juice and sports drinks have excessive osmolarity/sugar and inadequate sodium, worsening osmotic diarrhea.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Age-appropriate diet (including breastmilk/formula and complex carbohydrates) should resume as soon as rehydration is achieved.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Antidiarrheal motility agents like loperamide are contraindicated in young children due to paralytic ileus and respiratory depression risks.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 28-year-old male admitted to the inpatient behavioral health unit following a severe depressive episode with suicidal ideation.
clinical_scenario.assessment: After 3 days of appearing withdrawn and tearful, the client suddenly appears calm, cheerful, and gives his favorite wristwatch to another client.
medications: Sertraline 50 mg PO daily (started 3 days ago)

questions.stem: How should the nurse interpret this sudden improvement in mood and giving away of personal belongings?

options.text: The client may have made a definitive decision to end his life and now has the energy to carry out a plan; initiate 1:1 continuous observation immediately
Sertraline has achieved its full antidepressant therapeutic effect within 3 days; downgrade suicide precautions
The client is demonstrating healthy altruism and readiness for immediate hospital discharge
Ignore the behavior to reinforce positive mood changes

rationales.summary: An abrupt transition from deep despair to calm relief paired with giving away prized possessions is a classic warning sign of imminent suicidal intent.
rationales.A: Correct. Making the decision to die relieves internal ambivalence, and early antidepressant energy return (before mood lifts at 2-4 weeks) increases suicide execution risk; 1:1 observation is required.
rationales.B: Incorrect. SSRIs take 2 to 6 weeks for full mood improvement.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Giving away cherished items is a red flag for suicide preparation, not discharge readiness.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Failing to intervene places the client at imminent risk of self-harm.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 47-year-old male admitted 36 hours ago after a femur fracture; last drink of alcohol was 40 hours ago.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Agitated, diaphoretic, coarse hand tremors, reports seeing insects crawling on the walls; CIWA-Ar score is 22.
medications: Lorazepam 2 mg IV every 1 hour PRN CIWA-Ar > 15

questions.stem: Which medication is the primary first-line agent to prevent progression to delirium tremens and withdrawal seizures in this client?

options.text: Lorazepam (a benzodiazepine) titrated via symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar protocol
Haloperidol 5 mg IM monotherapy
Disulfiram 250 mg PO daily
Naltrexone 50 mg PO daily

rationales.summary: Benzodiazepines cross-react with GABA-A receptors to substitute for central nervous system alcohol depressant activity, preventing autonomic storm, seizures, and delirium tremens.
rationales.A: Correct. Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine therapy (lorazepam, diazepam, or chlordiazepoxide) is the gold-standard treatment for acute alcohol withdrawal.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not prevent delirium tremens.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Disulfiram is an aversive relapse-prevention drug used only after full detoxification.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Naltrexone reduces alcohol cravings post-detoxification and does not treat acute withdrawal.

questions.subtopic: Serotonin Syndrome vs. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 33-year-old female taking fluoxetine 40 mg daily who was recently prescribed tramadol and linezolid.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Agitated, diaphoretic, shivering, hyperreflexia (4+ patellar reflexes), inducible ankle clonus, dilated pupils.

questions.stem: Which neuromuscular assessment finding best distinguishes serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?

options.text: Hyperreflexia and inducible ankle clonus
Severe 'lead-pipe' generalized muscular rigidity with hyporeflexia
High fever and autonomic instability
Altered mental status and diaphoresis

rationales.summary: Both syndromes present with hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and altered mental status, but serotonin syndrome exhibits neuromuscular hyperactivity (hyperreflexia, clonus) whereas NMS produces lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia.
rationales.A: Correct. Clonus and hyperreflexia are hallmark neuromuscular features of serotonin toxicity (here triggered by SSRI + tramadol + MAOI-acting linezolid).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia characterize dopamine antagonist-induced NMS.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hyperthermia and autonomic dysregulation occur in both syndromes.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Agitation/delirium and diaphoresis occur in both conditions.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 26-year-old male admitted with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Staring intently toward the corner of the dayroom, whispering, and covering his ears; states, 'The voices are telling me that the staff are poisoning my lunch.'

questions.stem: Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?

options.text: I know those voices feel very real and frightening to you right now, though I do not hear them. Let's walk to a quieter area together.
Tell the voices to go away because nobody is poisoning your food.
What exactly are the voices saying about the kitchen staff?
You are hallucinating again because you stopped taking your risperidone.

rationales.summary: Therapeutic communication during auditory hallucinations validates the client's emotional experience while presenting reality calmly without reinforcing or arguing with the hallucination.
rationales.A: Correct. Empathy + reality orientation + offering a calming redirection builds trust and reduces anxiety without validating the delusion.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Arguing or dismissing the client's perception increases defensiveness and distrust.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Exploring the detailed content of hallucinations reinforces the psychotic experience.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Scolding or blaming the client impairs the therapeutic alliance.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: Medical-surgical nursing team consisting of an RN, an LPN/LVN, and an experienced unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) caring for four assigned clients.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Morning shift assignments are being delegated at 0715.

questions.stem: Which task is most appropriate for the registered nurse (RN) to delegate to the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?

options.text: Obtain routine vital signs and assist with ambulation for a client 2 days post-laparoscopic appendectomy who is stable
Perform the initial swallow screen on a newly admitted client with suspected acute ischemic stroke
Reinforce discharge teaching regarding warfarin dietary precautions with a client going home today
Monitor vital signs during the first 15 minutes of a packed red blood cell transfusion

rationales.summary: UAPs may perform routine, non-invasive, predictable tasks on stable clients; clinical assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable monitoring remain within the RN scope.
rationales.A: Correct. Routine vital signs and ambulation for a stable postoperative client are standard, safe UAP tasks.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Dysphagia screening requires clinical assessment judgment by an RN or speech-language pathologist.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Client education and evaluation of understanding require licensed nurse judgment.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The RN must remain with and assess the client during the critical first 15 minutes of a blood transfusion.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: Registered nurse on an acute medical-surgical step-down unit receiving morning shift report on four assigned clients.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Four clients require immediate attention after shift handoff.

vital_signs.Summary: Client 1: SpO2 95%; Client 2: HR 88 bpm; Client 3: Stridor; Client 4: Temp 37.9 C

questions.stem: Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client 4 hours post-anterior cervical discectomy who has developed high-pitched inspiratory stridor and neck fullness
A client with heart failure scheduled for morning furosemide whose serum potassium is 4.0 mEq/L
A client 2 days post-total knee replacement requesting oral pain medication for knee pain rated 6/10
A client with cellulitis whose intravenous cefazolin infusion pump is beeping 'infusion complete'

rationales.summary: Using the Airway-Breathing-Circulation prioritization framework, inspiratory stridor and neck swelling after anterior cervical surgery indicate acute airway compromise from a surgical hematoma.
rationales.A: Correct. Inspiratory stridor indicates severe upper airway narrowing that can progress rapidly to complete airway obstruction.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Normal potassium (4.0 mEq/L) and routine morning medication administration can wait until the airway threat is addressed.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Moderate postoperative pain is important but lower priority than an acute airway emergency.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A completed antibiotic infusion is non-urgent.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: 68-year-old female admitted with profuse watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping after completing a 10-day course of clindamycin.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Mild lower abdominal tenderness, skin intact.
medications: Oral vancomycin 125 mg PO four times daily x 10 days

questions.stem: Which infection control practices are mandatory when caring for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and running water rather than alcohol-based hand rub upon exiting the room
Wear a disposable isolation gown and gloves before entering the client's room
Use dedicated disposable or single-patient stethoscopes and blood pressure cuffs
Disinfect environmental surfaces with an EPA-registered sporicidal (bleach-based) disinfectant
Use alcohol-based hand sanitizer immediately after removing gloves to destroy C. difficile spores

rationales.summary: Clostridioides difficile forms hardy bacterial spores resistant to alcohol; mechanical friction with soap and water, gown/gloves, dedicated equipment, and bleach disinfection are required.
rationales.A: Correct. Soap and water friction physically removes C. difficile spores from hands.
rationales.B: Correct. Contact precautions (gown and gloves) prevent spore transfer onto uniforms and skin.
rationales.C: Correct. Dedicated equipment prevents cross-contamination between clients.
rationales.D: Correct. Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) sporicidal wipes are required to kill spores on high-touch surfaces.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores.

clinical_scenario.patient_profile: Emergency department nurse performing START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) mass-casualty triage following a multi-vehicle highway collision.
clinical_scenario.assessment: Four victims arrive simultaneously and are evaluated using Respirations, Perfusion, and Mental Status (RPM).

vital_signs.Summary: Victim 1: RR 34, radial pulse present, follows commands; Victim 2: Apneic even after head-tilt/jaw-thrust; Victim 3: RR 18, capillary refill 1 sec, obeys commands, closed radius fracture; Victim 4: RR 20, capillary refill 2 sec, obeys commands, bilateral femur fractures unable to walk

provider_orders: Assign START triage color tags (Red/Immediate, Yellow/Delayed, Green/Minor, Black/Expectant)

questions.stem: Assign the appropriate START mass-casualty triage tag to each victim.

rows.text: Victim 1: RR 34 breaths/min, radial pulse present, obeys commands
Victim 2: Apneic even after airway repositioning maneuver
Victim 3: Walking wounded with a closed forearm fracture, RR 18, cap refill 1 sec, alert
Victim 4: Non-ambulatory with bilateral femur fractures, RR 20, cap refill 2 sec, alert

rationales.summary: Under START triage: respiratory rate > 30, cap refill > 2 sec, or inability to follow commands = Red; persistent apnea after airway opening = Black; ambulatory = Green; non-ambulatory with normal RPM = Yellow.
rationales.V1: Red (Immediate): Respiratory rate > 30 breaths/min (34/min) places the victim in the Immediate category.
rationales.V2: Black (Expectant): Absence of spontaneous respirations after opening the airway classifies the victim as Expectant/Deceased in mass-casualty triage.
rationales.V3: Green (Minor): Ambulatory ('walking wounded') with intact RPM parameters.
rationales.V4: Yellow (Delayed): Unable to walk due to femur fractures, but RR < 30, cap refill <= 2 sec, and follows commands.
